1 And Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon because he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram had been a friend of David <note>original: "محبًا لداود" (muhibban li-Dawud) — literally "a lover of David," implying a deep personal and political alliance</note> all his days. 2 And Solomon sent word to Hiram, 3 saying, "You know that David my father was unable to build a house for the name of the Lord his God because of the wars that surrounded him, until the Lord placed his enemies under the soles of his feet. 4 But now the Lord my God has given me rest on every side, so that there is neither adversary nor evil occurrence. 5 And behold, I intend to build a house for the name of the Lord my God, just as the Lord spoke to David my father, saying, 'Your son, whom I will set in your place on your throne, he shall build the house for My name.' 6 Now therefore, command that they cut for me cedars from Lebanon. My servants will be with your servants, and I will give you the wages for your servants according to all that you say; for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians." <note>The Sidonians, inhabitants of the Phoenician city of Sidon, were renowned in antiquity for their skill in forestry and craftsmanship.</note>

7 When Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the Lord this day, who has given David a wise son over this great people." 8 And Hiram sent word to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message you sent to me. 1 And it came to pass after many days that the word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying, "Go, present yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain on the face of the earth." 
2 So Elijah went to present himself to Ahab; and there was a severe famine in Samaria. 
3 And Ahab had called Obadiah, who was in charge of the palace <note>literally "over the house"</note>. Now Obadiah feared the Lord greatly. 
4 For so it was, while Jezebel was cutting off the prophets of the Lord, that Obadiah had taken one hundred prophets and hidden them, fifty to a cave, and had sustained them with bread and water. 
5 And Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go into the land to all the springs of water and to all the valleys; perhaps we may find grass to keep the horses and mules alive, so that we will not lose all the livestock."

<margin>41</margin> Then he hurried to remove the bandage from his eyes; and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.
<margin>42</margin> And he said to him, "Thus says the Lord: 'Because you have let slip from your hand a man whom I had devoted to destruction <note>original: "ḥarramtahu" — referring to the 'Herem' or the ban, where a defeated enemy was designated as belonging to God for judgment rather than for political bargaining</note>, therefore your life shall go for his life, and your people for his people.'"
<margin>43</margin> So the king of Israel went to his house sullen and displeased, and came to Samaria.

<margin>22</margin> Now as for the people who remained in the land of Judah, whom **Nebuchadnezzar** king of Babylon had left, he appointed over them **Gedaliah** 
<margin>23</margin> the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan. * And when all the captains of the armies, they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, they came to Gedaliah at **Mizpah** <note>original: "al-Misfah"; an important administrative center north of Jerusalem</note>—namely Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan the son of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah the son of the Maachathite, they and their men. 
<margin>24</margin> * And Gedaliah swore to them and their men, and said to them, "Do not be afraid of the servants of the **Chaldeans** <note>original: "al-Kaldaniyyin"; the ruling ethnic group of the Babylonian Empire</note>. Dwell in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and it shall be 
<margin>25</margin> well with you." * But it happened in the seventh month that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal family, came with ten men and struck Gedaliah so that he died, along with the Jews and the Chaldeans 
<margin>26</margin> who were with him at Mizpah. * And all the people, from the small to the great, and the captains of the armies, arose and went to **Egypt**, for they were afraid of the Chaldeans.
<margin>27</margin> And it came to pass in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of **Jehoiachin** king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, that **Evil-merodach** <note>original: "Awil Marudakh"; the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar</note> king of Babylon, in the year that he 
<margin>28</margin> began to reign, released Jehoiachin king of Judah from prison. * And he spoke kindly to him and set his throne above the 
<margin>29</margin> thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon. * So he changed his prison garments, and he ate bread regularly 
<margin>30</margin> before him all the days of his life. * And as for his <term>allowance</term> <note>original: "wadhifatuhu"; literally his 'appointment' or 'ration'</note>, there was a continual allowance given him by the king, a portion for every day, all the days of his life.

## Chapter Eleven

1 Then all Israel gathered to David at Hebron, saying, “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh. <note>A biblical idiom expressing close kinship and tribal unity.</note> 
2 In times past, even when Saul was king, it was you who led Israel out to war and brought them back. And the Lord your God said to you, ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be a leader over my people Israel.’” * 
3 So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them in Hebron before the Lord. They anointed David king over Israel, according to the word of the Lord spoken by Samuel. <note>referring to the prophet Samuel, who originally anointed David in secret.</note>
4 And David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land. * 
5 And the inhabitants of Jebus said to David, “You shall not come in here.” Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, which is now the City of David. * 
6 And David said, “Whoever strikes the Jebusites first shall be chief and captain.” So Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first and became the chief. * 
7 Then David dwelt in the stronghold; therefore they called it the City of David. * 
8 And he built the city all around, from the citadel <note>original: "القلعة" (al-qal'ah), often identifying the "Millo," a defensive structure or terrace in ancient Jerusalem.</note> to the surrounding area, and Joab restored the rest of the city. * 
9 So David grew greater and greater, for the Lord of Hosts was with him.
10 Now these are the heads of the mighty men whom David had, who stood strongly with him in his kingdom, together with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the Lord concerning Israel. * 
11 And this is the number of the mighty men whom David had: Jashobeam the son of a Hachmonite, the chief of the captains; <note>original: "رئيس الثوالث" (ra'is al-thawalith), literally "chief of the thirds," a technical term for high-ranking military officers.</note> he brandished his spear against three hundred, whom he killed at one time. * 
12 And after him was Eleazar the son of Dodo the Ahohite, who was one of the three mighty men. * 
13 He was with David at Pas Dammim, <note>original: "فس دميم" (Pas Dammim), meaning "Boundary of Blood," a location between Socoh and Azekah.</note> and there the Philistines were gathered together for battle.

### Chapter Twenty-Three

<margin>1-2</margin> When David had grown old and full of days, he made his son Solomon king over Israel. And he gathered all the leaders of Israel, along with the priests and the Levites. 
<margin>3</margin> The Levites were numbered from the age of thirty years and upward, and their number by headcount, man by man, was thirty-eight thousand. 
<margin>4</margin> Of these, twenty-four thousand were to supervise the work of the house of the Lord, and six thousand were officials and judges. 
<margin>5</margin> Four thousand were gatekeepers, and four thousand offered praise to the Lord with the instruments <note>original: "الآلات" (al-alat); David is traditionally credited with inventing or commissioning specific musical instruments for Temple worship.</note> which were made for singing praise. 
<margin>6</margin> David divided them into divisions according to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. 
<margin>7-8</margin> From the Gershonites: Ladan and Shimei. The sons of Ladan: the chief was Jehiel, then Zetham, and Joel—three in all. 
<margin>9</margin> The sons of Shimei: Shelomith, Haziel, and Haran—three in all. These were the heads of the fathers' houses of Ladan. 
<margin>10</margin> And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These were the four sons of Shimei. 
<margin>11</margin> Jahath was the chief and Zizah was the second; but Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were counted as one father's house in the census. 
<margin>12</margin> The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel—four in all. The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart, he and his sons forever, to be sanctified as most holy, to burn incense <note>original: "يوقد" (yuqid); specifically the ritual act of kindling the sacred incense.</note> before the Lord, to minister to Him, and to give blessings in His name forever. 
<margin>14</margin> But as for Moses, the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi. 
<margin>15</margin> The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer. The son of Gershom: Shebuel the chief. 
<margin>17</margin> The son of Eliezer was Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many. 
<margin>19</margin> The son of Izhar: Shelomith the chief. The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth. 
<margin>20</margin> The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief and Isshiah the second. 
<margin>21</margin> The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish. 
<margin>22</margin> And Eleazar died and had no sons, only daughters; their cousins <note>original: "اخوتهنّ" (literally "their brothers"); in this genealogical context, it refers to kinsmen or cousins who married them to keep the inheritance within the family line.</note>, the sons of Kish, took them as wives. 
<margin>23</margin> The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth—three in all.

# Chapter Twenty-Four

<margin>1-2</margin> And these were the divisions of the sons of Aaron. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. But God said to me, 'You shall not build a house for My name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood.' <margin>4</margin> Yet the Lord, the God of Israel, chose me from all my father's house to be king over Israel forever. For He chose Judah as leader, and from the house of Judah, my father’s house, and among the sons of my father, He was pleased with me to make me king over all Israel. <margin>5</margin> And of all my sons—for the Lord has given me many sons—He has chosen my son Solomon to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the Lord over Israel. <margin>6</margin> He said to me, 'Solomon your son is the one who shall build My house and My courts, for I have chosen him to be My son, and I will be his Father. <margin>7</margin> I will establish his kingdom forever if he is steadfast in carrying out My commandments and My laws, as he is doing this day.' <margin>8</margin> Now therefore, in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the Lord, and in the hearing of our God, observe and seek out all the commandments of the Lord your God, so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your children after you forever. <margin>9</margin> And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve Him with a whole heart and a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every intent of the thoughts. ## Chapter Two

<margin>2:1-2</margin> Solomon commanded that a house be built for the name of the Lord and a palace for his own kingdom. Solomon counted out seventy thousand men to carry burdens and eighty thousand men to quarry stone in the mountains, with three thousand six hundred overseers to supervise them.

## Chapter Three

<margin>1</margin> Then Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where <margin>2</margin> the Lord had appeared to David his father, at the place David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. <margin>3</margin> He began to build on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign. These are the foundations Solomon laid for building the house of God: the length, according to the old standard of measurement <term>Cubits: the "old standard" or "first measure" refers to the ancient cubit, approximately 18 to 21 inches.</term>, was sixty cubits, and the width was twenty cubits. <margin>4</margin> The portico in front of the main hall was as long as the width of the house, twenty cubits, and its height was one hundred and twenty. He overlaid its inner surface with pure gold. <margin>5</margin> The main hall <margin>6</margin> he paneled with cypress wood and overlaid it with pure gold, and decorated it with palm tree designs and chains. He also <margin>7</margin> adorned the house with precious stones for beauty; the gold was gold of Parvaim <note>Parvaim is an unknown location, possibly in Arabia, famous for the highest quality of gold.</note>. He overlaid the house—its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors—with gold, and he engraved cherubim <term>Cherubim: celestial winged beings often depicted in ancient Near Eastern art as guardians of sacred spaces.</term> on the walls.

<margin>8</margin> He also made the most holy place <note>Commonly known as the "Holy of Holies," the innermost sanctuary of the Temple.</note>; its length corresponded to the width of the house, twenty cubits, and its width was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with six hundred talents <term>Talent: a large unit of weight; 600 talents of gold would be approximately 20 tons.</term> of fine gold. <margin>9</margin> The weight of the nails was fifty shekels of gold. He also overlaid the upper rooms with gold.

### Chapter Four

<margin>1</margin> And he made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high. <margin>2</margin> He also made the <term>Sea</term> <note>A massive bronze basin for ritual washing.</note> of cast metal, ten cubits from brim to brim, perfectly circular, and its height was five cubits, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. <margin>3</margin> And the likeness of <term>gourds</term> <note>Arabic: *qitha'*, likely referring to ornamental carvings.</note> was beneath it, encircling it for ten cubits around the Sea; the gourds were in two rows, cast as one piece with the Sea. <margin>4</margin> It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, three looking toward the west, three looking toward the south, and three looking toward the east; the Sea was placed upon them from above, and all their hindquarters were turned inward. <margin>5</margin> Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was fashioned like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It received and held three thousand <term>baths</term> <note>A Hebrew unit of liquid volume, approximately 22 liters per bath.</note>. <margin>6</margin> He also made ten basins and placed five on the right and five on the left for washing; in them they rinsed the items for the <term>burnt offering</term> <note>Arabic: *muhraqa*, a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire.</note>, but the Sea was for the priests to wash in. <margin>7</margin> And he made ten lampstands of gold according to their pattern and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.

### Chapter Fourteen

1 Then Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the City of David. His son Asa reigned in his place. In his days, the land was at peace for ten years. 2-3 Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the Lord his God. He removed the foreign altars and the <term>high places</term> <note>original: "المرتفعات" (al-murtafa'at). These were localized shrines or altars, often on hills, used for worship outside the central Temple in Jerusalem.</note>, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the <term>Asherah poles</term> <note>original: "السواري" (al-sawari). These were wooden cult objects dedicated to a Canaanite goddess.</note>. 4 He commanded Judah to seek the Lord, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandment. 5 He removed the high places and the incense altars <note>original: "تماثيل الشمس" (statues of the sun), likely referring to altars dedicated to solar deities.</note> from all the cities of Judah, and the kingdom was at peace under his rule. 6 He built fortified cities in Judah because the land was at peace. There was no war against him during those years, for the Lord had given him rest. 7 He said to Judah, "Let us build these cities and surround them with walls, towers, gates, and bars while the land is still before us, for we have sought the Lord our God. We sought Him, and He has given us rest on every side." So they built and prospered. 8 Asa had an army of three hundred thousand from Judah who carried large shields and spears, and two hundred and eighty thousand from Benjamin who carried small shields and drew bows. ## Chapter Twenty-Eight

1 **Ahaz** was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in **Jerusalem**. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the **Lord**, as his father **David** had done.
2 Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of **Israel** and even made cast idols for the **Baalim** <note>Baalim is the plural form of Baal, referring to various local manifestations of the Canaanite storm and fertility god.</note>.
3 He burned incense in the **Valley of Ben Hinnom** and burned his sons in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom the **Lord** had driven out before the people of **Israel**.
4 He offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
5 Therefore, the **Lord** his God delivered him into the hand of the king of **Aram** <note>Aram refers to the ancient kingdom of Syria, centered at Damascus.</note>. They defeated him and took many captives from him, bringing them to **Damascus**. He was also delivered into the hand of the king of **Israel**, who struck him with a great slaughter.
6 For **Pekah** son of **Remaliah** killed one hundred and twenty thousand in **Judah** in a single day—all of them valiant men—because they had forsaken the **Lord**, the God of their fathers.
7 **Zichri**, a mighty man of **Ephraim**, killed **Maaseiah** the king's son, **Azrikam** the officer in charge of the palace, and **Elkanah** the second-in-command to the king.
8 The Israelites took captive two hundred thousand of their relatives—women, sons, and daughters; they also took a great deal of plunder from them and brought the spoil to **Samaria**.
9 But a prophet of the **Lord** was there, whose name was **Oded**. 10 "And now you intend to subjugate the people of **Judah** and **Jerusalem** as your male and female slaves. But are you not also guilty of sins against the **Lord** your God?"
11 "Now hear me! Return the captives you took from your fellow Israelites, for the fierce anger of the **Lord** is upon you."
12 Then some of the leaders of the people of **Ephraim**—**Azariah** son of **Johanan**, **Berechiah** son of **Meshillemoth**, **Jehizkiah** son of **Shallum**, and **Amasa** son of **Hadlai**—stood up against those returning from the war.
13 They said to them, "You must not bring the captives here! For we are already guilty before the **Lord**, and you intend to add to our sins and our guilt. Our guilt is already great, and fierce anger is against **Israel**."
14 So the armed men left the captives and the plunder in front of the leaders and the whole assembly.
15 Then the men designated by name rose up and took the captives. From the plunder they clothed all who were naked; they provided them with clothes and sandals, gave them food and drink...

18 their God. As for the rest of the acts of Manasseh, his prayer to his God, and the words of the seers <term>Seers: prophets who received divine visions.</term> who spoke to him in the name of the Lord,

### Chapter Nine

<margin>1</margin> When these things were completed, the leaders approached me, saying: "The people of Israel, the priests, and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands, according to their abominations—from the Canaanites, the Hittites, 
<margin>2</margin> the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. * For they have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy seed has mixed with the peoples of the lands. 
<margin>3</margin> And the hand of the leaders and officials was foremost in this unfaithfulness." * When I heard this matter, I tore 
<margin>4</margin> my tunic and my robe, pulled out hair from my head and my beard, and sat down appalled. * Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel because of the unfaithfulness of the exiles gathered to me, while I sat 
<margin>5</margin> appalled until the evening offering. * At the evening offering, I rose from my humiliation, and with my tunic 
<margin>6</margin> and my robe torn, I fell on my knees and spread out my hands to the Lord my God. * And I said: "O my God, I am ashamed and embarrassed to lift up my face toward You, my God, for our iniquities have 
<margin>7</margin> increased over our heads, and our guilt has grown up to the heavens. * Since the days of our fathers, we have been in great guilt until this day. And for our iniquities, we, our kings, and our priests have been delivered into the hand of 
<margin>8</margin> the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plunder, and to humiliation of face, as it is this day. * And now, for a brief moment, grace has been shown from the Lord our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a stake in 
<margin>9</margin> His holy place, that our God may enlighten our eyes and give us a little reviving in our bondage. * For we are slaves; yet in our bondage our God has not forsaken us, but has extended mercy to us before the kings of Persia."

->Chapter Two<-

1 And it came to pass in the month of <term>Nisan</term><note>The first month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in the spring (March/April).</note>, in the twentieth year of King <term>Artaxerxes</term><note>original: "Artakhshasta". Refers to Artaxerxes I, the Persian monarch.</note>, when wine was before him, I took the wine and gave it to the king.
2 Now I had never been <term>sad</term><note>The Arabic "mukammadan" suggests a face heavy with grief or suppressed sorrow; it was often dangerous to show unhappiness in the presence of a monarch.</note> in his presence before. * So the king said to me, "Why is your face sad, since you are not sick? This is nothing but sorrow of heart." Then I was dreadfully afraid,
3 * and said to the king, "May the king live forever! Why should my face not be sad when the city, the place of my fathers' tombs, lies waste, and its gates are consumed by fire?"
4 * Then the king said to me, "What do you request?" So I prayed to the God of heaven,
5 * and I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor in your sight, that you send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' tombs, that I may rebuild it."
6 * Then the king said to me (the queen also sitting beside him), "How long will your journey be? And when will you return?" So it pleased the king to send me; and I set him a time.
7 * Furthermore I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given to me for the governors of the region <term>Beyond the River</term><note>A term for the Persian province of "Transeuphratia," which included the lands west of the Euphrates such as Syria and Palestine.</note>, that they may permit me to pass through until I come to Judah,
8 * and a letter to Asaph the keeper of the king’s <term>forest</term><note>original: "firdaws" (paradise/park). Referring to the royal timberlands or orchards.</note>, that he may give me timber..."

17 Then I said to them, "You see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lies waste, and its gates are burned with fire. Come and let us build the wall of Jerusalem, that we may no longer be a <term>reproach</term><note>A state of shame or disgrace in the eyes of neighboring nations.</note>." 18 And I told them of the hand of my God which had been good upon me, and also of the king’s words that he had spoken to me. So they said, "Let us rise up and build." Then they set their hands to this good work.

19 But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and <term>Geshem the Arab</term><note>A powerful leader of the Qedarite tribes who controlled the trade routes in the region.</note> heard it, they laughed at us and despised us, and said, "What is this thing that you are doing? Will you rebel against the king?" 20 So I answered them and said to them, "The God of heaven Himself will prosper us; therefore we His servants will arise and build, but you have no heritage or right or memorial in Jerusalem."

->Chapter Four<-

<margin>1</margin> And when Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he became angry and was greatly incensed, and he mocked <margin>2</margin> the Jews. He spoke before his brothers and the army of Samaria, saying, "What are these feeble Jews doing? Will they fortify themselves? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they finish in a day? Will they revive the stones from the heaps of rubbish—and they are burned?" <margin>3</margin> Now Tobiah the Ammonite was beside him, and he said, "Whatever they build, if even a fox <note>Tobiah uses the image of a small, light animal to mock the structural integrity of the Jewish repairs.</note> goes up on it, he will break down their stone wall." <margin>4</margin> "Hear, O our God, for we are despised; turn their reproach back on their own heads, and give them as plunder in a land of captivity! <margin>5</margin> Do not cover their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before You; for they have provoked You to anger before the builders." <margin>6</margin> So we built the wall, and the entire wall was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a heart <note>This indicates a spirit of willingness, resolve, and collective dedication to the task.</note> to work.

<margin>7</margin> When Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites <note>The Ashdodites were inhabitants of the Philistine city of Ashdod, representing the coastal opposition to the Jewish return from exile.</note> heard that the walls of Jerusalem were being repaired and the gaps <term>gaps</term><note>original: "الثغر" (al-thaghr) — refers to the breaches or broken sections of the defensive fortifications.</note> were beginning to be closed, they became very angry. <margin>8</margin> And they all conspired together to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause trouble there. <margin>9</margin> So we prayed to our God and set a guard against them day and night because of them. <margin>10</margin> And **Judah** <note>Referring here to the people of the province of Judah.</note> said, "The strength of the laborers is failing, and there is much rubbish; we are not able to build the wall." <margin>11</margin> And our enemies said, "They will not know or see until we come into their midst and kill them and stop the work." <margin>12</margin> And when the Jews who lived near them came, they told us ten times from all the places they had returned to us. <margin>13</margin> So I stationed the people in the lower parts of the space behind the wall and on the heights; I stationed them according to their families with their swords, their spears, and their bows. <margin>14</margin> And I looked and arose and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them; remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your houses." <margin>15</margin> When our enemies heard that we knew of their plot and that God had frustrated their counsel, we all returned to the wall, each to his own work. <margin>16</margin> From 그날 <note>From that day forward.</note> half of my servants worked on the construction while the other half held the spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail; and the leaders stood behind the whole house of **Judah**. <margin>17</margin> The builders on the wall and those who carried burdens loaded themselves so that they worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other. <margin>18</margin> Each of the builders had his sword strapped to his side as he built, and the one who blew the **trumpet** <note>original: "البوق" (al-buq) — likely the shofar, a ram's horn used for military signaling and assembly.</note> was beside me. <margin>19</margin> Then I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, "The work is great and extensive, and we are separated on the wall, far from one another. <margin>20</margin> In whatever place you hear the sound of the trumpet, gather there to us. Our God will fight for us." <margin>21</margin> So we continued the work, and half of them held spears from the break of dawn until the stars appeared. <margin>22</margin> At that time, I also said to the people, "Let every man and his servant stay overnight inside Jerusalem, so they may serve as guards for us by night and work by day." <margin>23</margin> Neither I, nor my brothers, nor my servants, nor the guards who followed me took off our clothes; each one went with his weapon even to the water <note>original: "الى الماء" — This suggests the men remained armed and ready even during personal washing or at the watering stations.</note>.

### Chapter Five

<margin>1-2</margin> And there was a great outcry of the people and their wives against their Jewish brothers. For there were <margin>3</margin> those who said, "Our sons and our daughters, we are many; let us get grain so that we may eat and live." And there were those <margin>4</margin> who said, "Our fields, our vineyards, and our houses we have mortgaged <note>During this period, the people were forced to pledge their ancestral lands as security for food during a famine.</note> so that we might get grain during the hunger." <margin>5</margin> And there were those who said, "We have borrowed money for the king’s tax <term>king’s tax</term><note>original: "خراج الملك" (kharaj al-malik) — the tribute or land tax required by the Persian Empire.</note> on our fields and our vineyards. And now, our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, and our children are like their children; yet here we are, forcing our sons and our daughters to be slaves, and some of our daughters are already enslaved. There is nothing in our power to do, for our fields and our vineyards belong to others."

<margin>6-7</margin> So I became very angry when I heard their outcry and these words. I consulted my own heart, and I rebuked the nobles and the rulers, and I said to them, "You are taking interest <term>interest</term><note>original: "الربا" (al-riba) — also translated as usury. Mosaic law forbade Israelites from charging interest to one another on essential loans.</note>, every one from his brother." And I called a great assembly against them. <margin>8</margin> And I said to them, "We have bought back our Jewish brothers who were sold to the nations, according to our ability. And yet you yourselves sell your brothers, so that they must be sold back to us?" And they were silent and found no answer. <margin>9</margin> Then I said, "The thing you are doing is not good. Should you not walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the nations, our enemies? <margin>10</margin> I also, and my brothers and my servants, have lent them money and grain. Let us now abandon this interest. <margin>11</margin> Restore to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive groves, and their houses, and the hundredth part of the money, the grain, the wine, and the oil that you are taking from them as interest." <margin>12</margin> Then they said, "We will restore them and will demand nothing from them; we will do exactly as you say." So I called the priests and made them swear an oath to do according to this word. <margin>13</margin> Then I shook out my lap <note>original: "حجري" (hujri) — referring to the fold of the garment used as a pocket; this was a symbolic gesture of emptying or casting someone out.</note> and said, "So may God shake out every man from his house and from his labor who does not keep this word; even so may he be shaken out and emptied." And all the assembly said, "Amen," and praised the Lord. And the people did according to this word.

<margin>14</margin> Moreover, from the day that I was appointed to be their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year to the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes <note>Artaxerxes I was the Persian king who authorized Nehemiah's mission to Jerusalem.</note>—twelve years—neither I nor my brothers ate the governor's food allowance. <margin>15</margin> But the former governors who were before me laid heavy burdens on the people, and took from them bread and wine, besides forty shekels <term>shekels</term><note>A standard unit of weight for silver used as currency.</note> of silver. Even their servants lorded it over the people. But I did not do so, because of the fear [of God].

<vocab>Nehemiah, the Jews, interest (usury), Artaxerxes, the governor, shekels</vocab>

## Chapter Six

1 Now when it was heard by Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies that I had built the wall and that no breach remained in it—though at that time I had not yet set up the leaves of the gates— 2 Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, "Come, let us meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono." But they were planning to do me harm. 3 So I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work, so I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?" 4 And they sent to me this message four times, and I answered them in the same way.

5 Then Sanballat sent his servant to me with the same message a fifth time, with an <term>open letter</term><note>Sending a letter "open" (unsealed) was a deliberate insult in the ancient Near East, intended to allow the contents—in this case, rumors of treason—to be read by the public and spread as gossip.</note> in his hand. 6 In it was written: "It is heard among the nations, and Gashmu <note>original: "جشم" (Jasham) — a variation of the name Geshem.</note> says, that you and the Jews are planning to rebel; that is why you are building the wall. And according to these reports, you are to become their king. 7 You have also appointed prophets to proclaim about you in Jerusalem, saying, 'There is a king in Judah!' And now these words will be reported to the king. So come now, let us consult together." 8 Then I sent to him, saying, "No such things as you say are happening; you are merely inventing them from your own heart." 9 For they were all trying to frighten us, saying, "Their hands will drop the work, and it will not be done." But now, O God, strengthen my hands.

10 Then I went to the house of Shemaiah the son of Delaiah, the son of Mehetabel, who was confined to his home. He said, "Let us meet in the house of God, inside the temple, and let us close the doors of the temple, for they are coming to kill you; indeed, they are coming to kill you at night."

<summary>Nehemiah concludes his selfless tenure as governor and faces a series of deceptive invitations and false accusations of rebellion from Sanballat and his allies.</summary>

11 "at night they are coming to kill you." But I said, "Should a man such as I flee? And who like me could go into the Temple and live? <note>Under Jewish Law, only priests were permitted to enter the inner parts of the Temple; for Nehemiah, a layman, to enter would be a sacrilegious act punishable by death, or at least one that would destroy his reputation.</note> I will not go in." 12 Then I realized, and behold, God had not sent him, for he spoke this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. 13 For this reason he was hired, that I might be afraid and do so and sin, that they might have an evil report to reproach me. 14 Remember, O my God, Tobiah and Sanballat according to these works of theirs, and the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who tried to make me afraid.

15 So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth of <term>Elul</term><note>The sixth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly corresponding to August/September.</note>, in fifty-two days. 16 And when all our enemies heard of it, and all the nations around us saw it, they were greatly cast down in their own eyes, and they knew that this work had been done by our God. 17 Moreover, in those days many of the nobles of Judah sent letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters came to them. 18 For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berekiah. 19 They also reported his good deeds before me and brought my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.

I stationed some of my servants at the gates, so that no load might be brought in on the Sabbath day. * <margin>20</margin> Then the merchants and sellers of all kinds of merchandise spent the night outside Jerusalem once or twice. * <margin>21</margin> But I warned them and said to them, "Why do you spend the night in front of the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you." From that time on, they did not come on the Sabbath. * <margin>22</margin> And I commanded the Levites to purify themselves and come and guard the gates to keep the Sabbath day holy. **6** [The garden was decorated] with cords of **fine white linen** <note>original: "بزّ" (bazz) referring to high-quality, bleached linen cloth</note> and **purple** <note>original: "ارجوان" (urjuwan) - a dye extracted from sea snails, so expensive it was reserved for royalty</note> attached to silver rings and marble pillars. **10** On the seventh day, when the King’s heart was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas—the **seven eunuchs** <note>Trusted court officials who managed the private royal quarters</note> who served King Ahasuerus— **11** to bring Queen Vashti before the King wearing her royal crown, in order to show her beauty to the people and the princes, for she was very lovely to look at. **12** But Queen Vashti **refused to come** at the King’s command delivered by the eunuchs. At this, the King became greatly incensed, and his anger burned within him.

**13** Then the King spoke to the **wise men** who understood the times—for this was the King’s custom to consult all who were experts in law and justice. **14** Those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the **seven princes of Persia and Media** who had access to the King’s presence and held the highest rank in the kingdom. **15** "According to the **law**," <note>original: "السُنّة" (al-sunnah) here meaning established legal custom or decree</note> he asked, "what must be done with Queen Vashti, because she has not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs?"

**16** Then Memucan spoke in the presence of the King and the princes: "Queen Vashti has wronged not only the King, but also all the princes and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. **17** For the news of the Queen’s conduct will reach all women, causing them to **despise their husbands** in their own eyes, as they will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she would not come.' **18** This very day, the noble women of Persia and Media who have heard of the Queen’s conduct will say the same to all the King’s princes, and there will be no end of contempt and wrath. **19** If it pleases the King, let a **royal decree** go out from him, and let it be recorded in the laws of Persia and Media—which cannot be changed—that Vashti is never again to enter the presence of King Ahasuerus..."

## Chapter Two

**1** After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus had subsided, he remembered Vashti, what she had done, and what had been decreed against her. **2** Then the King’s servants who attended him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the King. **3** And let the King appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather all the beautiful young virgins to **Shushan the Palace** <note>Also known as Susa, one of the capitals of the Persian Empire</note>, to the harem <note>original: "بيت النساء" (bayt al-nisa) – literally 'the house of women'</note>, under the care of **Hegai**, the King’s eunuch, guardian of the women. Let their beauty treatments be given to them. **4** And let the young woman who pleases the King be queen instead of Vashti." This proposal was pleasing in the eyes of the King, and he did so.

**5** Now in **Shushan the Palace** there was a certain Jewish man whose name was **Mordecai**, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of **6** Kish, a Benjamite, who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been exiled with **Jeconiah** <note>original: "يكنيا" – referring to King Jehoiachin of Judah</note>, king of Judah, whom **Nebuchadnezzar** the king of Babylon had captured. **7** And he was the guardian of **Hadassah** <note>A Hebrew name meaning 'myrtle'</note>, that is, **Esther**, his uncle’s daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was lovely in form and beautiful **8** to look at. When her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter. So it was, when the King’s command and decree were heard, and many young women were gathered to Shushan the Palace under the care of Hegai, **9** that Esther also was taken to the King’s palace, into the care of Hegai, the guardian of the women. The young woman pleased him and found favor in his sight. So he quickly provided her with beauty treatments and her special portions <note>Refers to prescribed royal rations or diets</note>, and gave her seven choice young women from the King’s palace. He then moved her and her young women to the best place in the harem.

## Chapter Three

**1** After these events, King **Ahasuerus** promoted **Haman** the son of Hammedatha the **Agagite**, **2** and advanced him and set his seat above all the princes who were with him. All the King’s servants who were at the King’s gate would bow down and prostrate themselves before Haman, for so the King had commanded concerning him. **3** But **Mordecai** would not bow down nor prostrate himself. Then the King’s servants who were at the King’s gate said **4** to Mordecai, “Why do you transgress the King’s command?” When they spoke to him day after day and he would not listen to them, they informed Haman to see if Mordecai’s reasonings would stand; for he had told them that he was a **Jew**.

**5-6** When Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or prostrate himself before him, Haman was filled with rage. But he thought it beneath him <note>original: "وازدرى في عينيه" — literally 'it was despicable in his eyes'</note> to lay hands on Mordecai alone, for they had told him of Mordecai’s people. Therefore, Haman sought to destroy all the Jews who were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus—the people of Mordecai.

**7** In the first month, which is the month of **Nisan**, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast the **Pur** <note>original: "فوراً" (fawran) — meaning a lot or dice used for divination; the text explains this as "قرعة" (qur'a), a lot</note>, before Haman from day to day and from month to month, until the twelfth month, which is the month of **Adar**.

**8** Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom; their laws are different from those of all other peoples, and they do not observe the King’s laws. Therefore, it is not fitting for the King to let them remain. **9** If it pleases the King, let it be decreed that they be destroyed, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who perform the work, to be brought into the King’s treasuries.”

**10** So the King took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. **11** The King said to Haman, “The silver is given to you, and the people also, to do with them as seems good in your eyes.”

## Chapter Six

<margin>1-3</margin> Then Job answered and said: * Oh, that my grief were weighed, and my calamity laid in the scales <margin>3-4</margin> together! For now it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash. <note>original: "لغا كلامي" (lagha kalami). This suggests words spoken in haste or without composure due to extreme pressure.</note> * For <margin>5</margin> the arrows of the Almighty <term>Al-Qadir: The Almighty</term> are within me; my spirit drinks their poison. The terrors of God are set in array against me. * Does the <margin>6</margin> wild donkey bray when it has grass? Or does the ox low over its fodder? * Can that which is tasteless be eaten without salt? Or is there any <margin>7</margin> flavor in the juice of the mallow? <note>original: "مرق البقلة" (marq al-baqlah) — Interpreted variously as the white of an egg or the broth of a tasteless herb (like purslane). Job uses this to describe his insufferable and "tasteless" existence.</note> * My soul refuses to touch them; they are like loathsome food to me. <margin>8-9</margin> Oh, that my request might come to pass, and that God would grant me my hope! * That it would please God to <margin>10</margin> crush me; that He would loose His hand and cut me off! * Then I would still have comfort; I would rejoice in unsparing pain, for I have not denied the words of the Holy One. <margin>11</margin> What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should prolong <margin>12</margin> my life? * Is my strength the strength of stones? Is my flesh bronze? * Is it not <margin>13</margin> that I have no help within me, and success is driven from me?
<margin>14-15</margin> Kindness is due to the despairing from his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty. * But my brothers have been treacherous like a wadi; <note>original: "الغدير... ساقية الوديان" — A wadi is a seasonal stream that flows violently during the rains but dries up completely in the summer, leaving travelers disappointed.</note> like the stream of the valleys they pass away, <margin>16</margin> which are dark because of the <margin>17</margin> ice, and into which the snow hides itself. * When they flow, they vanish; when it is hot, they dry up from <margin>18-19</margin> their place. * The paths of their way turn aside; they go into the waste and perish. * The caravans of Tema <note>Tema: An oasis in northwest Arabia, a major trade center.</note> looked; <margin>20-21</margin> the travelers of Sheba <note>Sheba: A kingdom in south Arabia (modern Yemen), known for its wealthy merchants.</note> hoped for them. * They were disappointed because they had been confident; they came there and were confounded. * For now <margin>22</margin> you are like them; you see my terror and are afraid. * Did I say, "Give me something"? Or, "Offer a <margin>23</margin> bribe for me from your wealth"? * Or, "Deliver me from the enemy’s hand"? Or, "Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless"? <margin>24-25</margin> * Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have erred. * How forceful are right words! But what does your <margin>26</margin> reproof prove? * Do you intend to reprove words, when the speech of the desperate is for the wind? <margin>27</margin> * You would even cast lots over the orphan, and dig a pit for your friend.

<summary>Job responds to Eliphaz by justifying his lament, describing his suffering as a heavy burden and God’s arrows as poisonous. He criticizes his friends for their lack of empathy, comparing their fickle support to seasonal streams that dry up when most needed.</summary>

### Chapter Nine

<margin>1-2</margin> Then Job answered and said: * "Truly, I know it is so. But how can a man be righteous 
<margin>3-4</margin> before God? * If one wished to contend with Him, he could not answer Him once in a thousand times. * He is wise in heart 
<margin>5</margin> and mighty in strength. Who has hardened himself against Him and remained safe? * He who removes the mountains and they do not know it, 
<margin>6-7</margin> when He overturns them in His anger. * He who shakes the earth out of its place, so that its pillars tremble. * He who commands the sun 
<margin>8</margin> and it does not rise; who seals up the stars. * He who alone stretched out the heavens and walked upon the heights 
<margin>9</margin> of the sea. * He is the Maker of the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, <note>original: "النعش والجبار والثريا" — these Arabic names refer to the Great Bear (Ursa Major), the Giant (Orion), and the Seven Sisters (Pleiades).</note> and the chambers of the south. 
<margin>10</margin> * He performs great deeds that cannot be searched out, and wonders without number.
<margin>11</margin> * Behold, He passes by me, and I do not see Him; He moves on, and I do not perceive Him. 
<margin>12</margin> * If He snatches away, who can stop Him? Who can say to Him, 'What are you doing?' 
<margin>13</margin> * God does not restrain His anger; beneath Him the helpers of Rahab <term>Rahab: a primordial sea monster or chaos-dragon in ancient Near Eastern mythology</term> bow down. 
<margin>14</margin> * How then could I answer Him? Or choose my words to argue with Him? 
<margin>15</margin> * Though I were in the right, I could not answer; I could only plead for mercy from my Judge."

<summary>Bildad concludes his speech by arguing that the wicked are as fragile as a spider's web while the righteous will be restored. Job responds by acknowledging God's overwhelming majesty and the futility of a human trying to justify themselves before an all-powerful Creator.</summary>

### Chapter Ten

١-٢ My soul loathes my life. I will give free rein to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul, * saying to God: "Do not condemn me; let me know why You contend with me."

## Chapter Eleven

<margin>١-٢</margin> Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Should a multitude of words go unanswered? Or should a man of many words <note>original: "رجل مهذار" (rajul mihdhār) — a babbler or a talkative person who speaks without substance.</note> be justified?
<margin>٣-٤</margin> Should your empty talk silence men? Should you mock and no one shame you? For you say, 'My teaching is pure
<margin>٥-٦</margin> and I am clean in your eyes.' But oh, that God would speak, and open His lips against you, and reveal to you the secrets of wisdom, for true understanding is manifold. Know then that God exacts from you less than your guilt deserves.
<margin>٧-٨</margin> Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you reach the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than the heavens—
<margin>٩</margin> what can you do? Deeper than the Abyss <term>al-hāwiyah: the underworld or the realm of the dead, often used to describe the deepest, most unknowable depths</term>, what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth
<margin>١٠</margin> and broader than the sea. If He passes by and imprisons or convenes a court, who can turn Him back? For He knows

<margin>١٥</margin> in your hand, and let no injustice dwell in your tents; then you could lift up your face without spot.
<margin>١٦ ١٧</margin> You would be steadfast and not fear. For you would forget your misery; you would remember it as waters that have passed away. And brighter
<margin>١٨</margin> than the noonday your life would rise; even the darkness would become like the morning. You would be secure because there is hope; you would look
<margin>١٩</margin> around you and lie down in safety. You would lie down, and none would make you afraid; many would entreat your favor.
<margin>٢٠</margin> But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and their refuge will perish; their only hope is the breathing out of their last."

<summary>Job concludes his lament by wishing he had never been born, while Zophar enters the debate with a stern rebuke, claiming that God's wisdom is beyond Job's reach and that Job's suffering is actually lighter than his sins deserve.</summary>

## Chapter Twenty-Four

<margin>1-2</margin> Why, since times are not hidden from the Almighty, do those who know Him not see His days? <note>Job asks why God, who sees all time, does not set a public schedule for judging the wicked.</note> They move the <term>boundary markers</term> <note>original: "التخوم" (al-tukhum). In the ancient Near East, moving a neighbor's boundary stone was a grave crime equivalent to land theft.</note>.
<margin>3-4</margin> They seize a flock and pasture it. They drive away the donkey of the orphans and take the widow’s ox as a pledge. They push the poor off the path.
<margin>5</margin> The poor of the land hide themselves together. Look, like <term>wild donkeys</term> <note>original: "الفراء" (al-fara'). A metaphor for those forced into a lawless, scavenging existence on the margins of society.</note> in the wilderness, they go out to their work, rising early for food. The wasteland provides bread for their children.
<margin>6</margin> In the field they harvest their fodder, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked.
<margin>7</margin> They spend the night naked, without clothing, and they have no covering in the cold.
<margin>8</margin> They are drenched by the rain of the mountains, and for lack of shelter, they huddle against the rock.
<margin>9-10</margin> They snatch the orphan from the breast, and take pledges from the poor. They go about naked, without clothing, and though hungry, they carry the sheaves.
<margin>11</margin> They press out oil within their walls; they tread the winepresses, yet they thirst.
<margin>12</margin> From the city, men groan, and the soul of the wounded cries out for help; yet God does not pay attention to the wrongdoing.
<margin>13</margin> These are among those who rebel against the light; they do not know its ways, nor do they abide in its paths.
<margin>14</margin> At daybreak the murderer rises to kill the poor and the needy, and in the night he is like a thief.
<margin>15</margin> The eye of the adulterer watches for the twilight, saying, "No eye shall see me," and he puts a veil on his face.
<margin>16</margin> In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in. They do not know the light.
<margin>17</margin> For to them, the morning is as the shadow of death; for they are familiar with the terrors of the shadow of death.
<margin>18</margin> He is swift on the face of the waters; their portion in the land is cursed. No one turns toward the path of the vineyards.
<margin>19</margin> Drought and heat consume the snow waters; so does the <term>Abyss</term> <note>original: "الهاوية" (al-hawiyah). Referring to Sheol or the grave, the place of the dead.</note> those who have sinned.
<margin>20</margin> The womb forgets him; the worm finds him sweet. He is remembered no more, and wickedness is broken like a tree.
<margin>21</margin> He wrongs the barren woman who does not bear, and does no good for the widow.
<margin>22</margin> He drags away the mighty by his power; he rises up, and no one is sure of life.
<margin>23</margin> He gives them security and they rely on it, but His eyes are upon their ways.
<margin>24</margin> They are exalted for a little while, then they are gone; they are brought low. Like all others, they are gathered up; they are cut off like the heads of grain.
<margin>25</margin> And if it is not so, who will prove me a liar and make my words of no account?

<summary>Job laments the apparent absence of divine justice, describing how the wicked exploit the vulnerable and commit crimes under the cover of darkness while God remains seemingly indifferent. He concludes by challenging anyone to disprove his observation that the wicked often prosper before their eventual end.</summary>

<summary>Elihu argues that God is inherently just and sovereign, maintaining that He does not need to justify His actions to men and that Job’s complaints show a lack of wisdom. He concludes by accusing Job of adding defiant rebellion to his initial sins by questioning God's governance.</summary>

## Psalm 13
->To the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David.<-

1 How long, O Lord? Will You forget me completely? How long will You hide Your face from me?
2 How long shall I take counsel <note>literally "put worries" or "place anxieties" (aj'al humuman).</note> in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? How long will my enemy be exalted over me?
3 Look and answer me, O Lord my God; enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;
4 Lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed against him"; lest my oppressors rejoice when I am shaken.
5-6 But I have trusted in Your mercy; my heart shall rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the Lord, because He has dealt bountifully with me.

## Psalm 14
->To the Chief Musician. Of David.<-

1 The fool has said in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they have done abominable deeds; there is no one who does good.
2 The Lord looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there are any who understand, who seek God.
3 They have all turned aside, they have together become corrupt; there is no one who does good, no, not even one.
4 Do all the workers of iniquity have no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon the Lord?
5-6 There they were in great fear, for God is in the generation of the righteous. You have frustrated the plans of the poor, but the Lord is his refuge.
7 Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! <note>Zion is the hill in Jerusalem often used to represent the city's spiritual heart.</note> When the Lord restores the captivity of His people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad.

## Psalm 42

### To the Chief Musician. A Contemplation <term>original: "قصيدة" (qaṣīdah) — used here to translate the Hebrew "Maschil," a literary or musical term for a meditative or instructive poem</term> of the sons of Korah.

1 As the deer pants <note>original: "يشتاق" (yashtāqu) — to long for or desire. The image is of a parched animal searching for a stream during a drought.</note> for the water brooks, so my soul pants for You, O God.
2 * My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?
3-4 * My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all day long, "Where is your God?" * These things I remember as I pour out my soul within me: how I used to walk with the multitude <term>original: "الجمّاع" (al-jummā‘) — a crowd or festive gathering</term>, processing with them to the house of God with the voice of joy and praise, a multitude keeping the festival.
5 * Why are you cast down <note>original: "منحنية" (manḥaniyah) — literally "bent over" or "bowed down" in grief.</note>, O my soul? And why are you disquieted <note>original: "تئنّين" (ta’innīn) — to groan, moan, or be in a state of inner turmoil.</note> within me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise Him for the help of His countenance.
6 * O my God, my soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember You from the land of the Jordan, and from the heights of Hermon <term>Mount Hermon: the highest mountain range in the region, located at the northern source of the Jordan River</term>, from the hill of Mizar <note>original: "مصعر" (muṣ‘ar) — meaning "smallness"; likely a specific minor peak in the Hermon range.</note>.
7 * Deep calls unto deep at the noise of Your waterfalls <term>original: "ميازيبك" (mayāzībika) — literally "water-spouts" or channels</term>; all Your waves and billows have gone over me.
8 * In the daytime the Lord will command His lovingkindness, and in the night His song shall be with me—a prayer to the God of my life.
9 * I will say to God my Rock <term>original: "صخرتي" (ṣakhratī) — a common biblical metaphor for God as a steady, unshakeable refuge</term>, "Why have You forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"
10 * As with a crushing in my bones, my enemies reproach me, while they say to me all day long, "Where is your God?"
11 * Why are you cast down, O my soul? And why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God; for I shall yet praise Him, the help of my countenance and my God.

## Psalm 43

1 Vindicate me, O God, and plead my cause against an unmerciful nation; deliver me from the deceitful and unjust man.
2 * For You are the God of my strength <term>original: "حصني" (ḥuṣnī) — my fortress or stronghold</term>. Why have You cast me off? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?
3 * Oh, send out Your light and Your truth! Let them lead me; let them bring me to Your holy hill and to Your tabernacles.
4 * Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy; and on the harp <term>original: "العود" (al-‘ūd) — the oud or lute; used here to translate the biblical lyre</term> I will praise You, O God, my God.
5 * Why are you cast down, O my soul? And why are you disquieted within me? Hope in God; for I shall yet praise Him, the help of my countenance and my God.

## A Psalm. Of Asaph. <note>Asaph was a prominent Levite singer and musician appointed by King David to lead the choral worship in the Tabernacle.</note>

<margin>1-2</margin> God, the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting * From

<margin>4</margin> and around Him is a great tempest * He calls the heavens from above and the earth, that He may judge His people.
<margin>5-6</margin> * Gather to Me My godly ones, who have made My covenant by sacrifice * And the heavens declare His justice,
for God Himself is the Judge. Selah <term>original: "سلاه" (Selah) — a musical or liturgical pause for reflection</term>.
<margin>7-8</margin> Hear, O My people, and I will speak; O Israel, and I will testify against you. I am God, your God * Not for
<margin>9</margin> your sacrifices do I rebuke you; for your burnt offerings are continually before Me * I will not take from your house
<margin>10</margin> a bull, nor from your folds any goats * For every beast of the forest is Mine, and the cattle upon the mountains
<margin>11</margin> by the thousands * I know every bird of the mountains, and the wild beasts of the field are with Me * If I were hungry, I would
<margin>12</margin> not tell you, for the world is Mine and all its fullness * Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood
<margin>14</margin> of goats? * Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High * And call upon Me in the day of trouble;
I will deliver you, and you shall glorify Me.
<margin>16</margin> But to the wicked, God says: What right have you to recount My statutes and carry My covenant upon your lips?
<margin>17</margin> * Seeing you have hated discipline and cast My words behind you * When you saw a thief,
<margin>19</margin> you consented with him, and your portion was with adulterers * You have released your mouth for evil, and your tongue frames deceit.
<margin>20</margin> * You sit and speak against your brother; against your own mother’s son you place a stumbling block * These things you have done, and I kept silent.
<margin>22</margin> You thought that I was just like you. I will rebuke you and set your sins in order before your eyes * Understand... <note>The text here ends abruptly, likely continuing on the following page with the final warning to those who forget God.</note>

## The Fifty-First Psalm

->For the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David when Nathan the prophet came to him after he had gone in to Bathsheba<- <note>This heading provides the historical context for the psalm: King David’s profound regret and plea for forgiveness after his adultery with Bathsheba and the subsequent murder of her husband, Uriah, were exposed by the prophet Nathan.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your mercy; according to the abundance of Your compassion, blot out my transgressions.
<margin>2-3</margin> * Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin * For I acknowledge my transgressions,
<margin>4</margin> and my sin is ever before me * Against You, You only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in Your sight;
<margin>5</margin> so that You are justified in Your words and blameless in Your judgment * Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. <note>This verse is often cited in theological discussions regarding the inherent nature of human fallibility.</note>
<margin>6-7</margin> Behold, You desire truth in the inward parts, and in the hidden part You will make me to know wisdom * Purge me with hyssop <term>original: "الزوفا" (al-zufa) — a small bushy plant used in ancient Middle Eastern purification rituals to sprinkle water or blood</term>, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow * Let me hear joy and gladness;
<margin>8</margin> that the bones You have broken may rejoice * Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.
<margin>9</margin> Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.
<margin>10</margin> Do not cast me away
<margin>11</margin> from Your presence, and do not take Your Holy Spirit from me *
<margin>12</margin> Restore to me the joy of Your salvation,
<margin>13</margin> and uphold me with a willing spirit * Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners shall return to You.
<margin>14</margin> Deliver me from bloodguilt <note>original: "الدماء" (the bloods) — a reference to the guilt of causing another's death, specifically Uriah the Hittite in David's case</note>, O God, the God of my salvation; and my tongue shall sing aloud of Your righteousness *
<margin>15</margin> O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare Your praise *
<margin>16</margin> For You do not delight in sacrifice, otherwise I would give it;
<margin>17</margin> You are not pleased with burnt offerings * The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise.
<margin>18</margin> Do good in Your good pleasure to Zion; build the walls of Jerusalem *
<margin>19</margin> Then You will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then they shall offer bulls on Your altar.

### The Fifty-Sixth Psalm

->To the Chief Musician. Set to "The Silent Dove among Strangers." A Miktam of David when the<-
->Philistines seized him in Gath.<-
<note>The phrase "The Silent Dove among Strangers" (Al-Hamama al-Bakma' bayna al-Ghuraba') likely refers to the melody or the specific tune to which this psalm was set.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Be merciful to me, O God, for man would swallow me up; all day long the warrior oppresses me. 
<margin>2-3</margin> * My enemies would swallow me up all day long, for many are those who fight against me in pride. * In the day when I am afraid, 
<margin>4</margin> I will trust in You. * In God—I will praise His word—in God I have put my trust; I will not fear. What can 
<margin>5-6</margin> flesh do to me? * All day long they twist my words; all their thoughts are against me for evil. * They gather 
<margin>7</margin> themselves together, they hide themselves, they mark my steps, as they lie in wait for my soul. * Shall they escape by iniquity? In Your anger 
<margin>8</margin> cast down the peoples, O God! * You number my wanderings; put my tears into Your bottle. 
Are they not in Your book?
<margin>9</margin> Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call; this I know, because 
<margin>10</margin> God is for me. * In God—I will praise His word—in the Lord—I will praise His word— * In God I have put my trust; I will not be afraid. 
<margin>11</margin> What can man do to me? * Your vows are upon me, O God; I will render thank-offerings to You,

## Psalm Seventy-Three

### A Psalm of Asaph <note>Asaph was a prominent Levite singer and musician appointed by King David; he is credited with twelve psalms that often grapple with communal or philosophical difficulties.</note>

<margin>1-2</margin> Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. * But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled;
<margin>3</margin> my steps had nearly slipped. * For I was envious of the arrogant <note>original: المتكبرين - 'al-mutakabbirin,' referring to those who are boastful or proud.</note> when I saw the prosperity of
<margin>4-5</margin> the wicked. * For there are no pangs in their death, and their bodies are fat. * They are not in the trouble of 
<margin>6</margin> men, nor are they stricken along with mankind. * Therefore pride is their necklace; they clothe themselves with the garment of their violence.
<margin>7-8</margin> * Their eyes bulge out from fatness; they have surpassed the imaginings of the heart. * They scoff and speak
<margin>9</margin> with evil oppression; from on high they speak. * They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongues walk
<margin>10</margin> through the earth. * Therefore his people return here, and like overflowing waters they are drained by them. * And they say,
<margin>11</margin> “How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High?” <note>original: العلي - 'al-Ali,' a title for God meaning the Most High or the Exalted.</note> * Behold, these are the wicked; always
<margin>12</margin> at ease, they increase in wealth.
<margin>13-14</margin> Truly in vain I have kept my heart pure and washed my hands in innocence. * For all day long I have been stricken,
<margin>15</margin> and punished every morning. * If I had said, “I will speak thus,” I would have been untrue to the generation 
<margin>16-17</margin> of Your children. * But when I thought how to understand this, it was wearisome in my eyes; * until I entered
<margin>18</margin> the sanctuary of God and perceived their end. * Truly You set them in slippery places; You cast them down to
<margin>19-20</margin> ruin <note>original: البوار - 'al-buwar,' referring to destruction or perishing.</note>. * How they are destroyed in a moment! They are utterly swept away by terrors <note>original: الدواهي - 'al-dawahi,' meaning great calamities or disasters.</note>. * Like a dream when
one awakes, O Lord, when You awake, You will despise their phantom image.
<margin>21-22</margin> For my heart was embittered, and I was pierced in my kidneys <note>original: كليتيّ - 'kilyatayya,' literally 'my kidneys.' <margin>23-24</margin> like a beast before You. * Nevertheless I am continually with You; You hold my right hand. * You guide me

<margin>26</margin> nothing on earth. * My flesh and my heart fail; God is the rock of my heart and my portion 
<margin>27-28</margin> forever. * For behold, those who are far from You shall perish; You destroy everyone who is unfaithful to You. * But...

<note>Psalm 119 is a giant acrostic poem. In the original Hebrew, each section consists of eight verses starting with the same letter of the alphabet. The Arabic translation marks these sections with the corresponding letters.</note>

# Psalm 141

->A Psalm of David<-

1 O Lord, I cry out to You; make haste to me! Give ear to my voice when I cry
2 to You. * Let my prayer be set before You as incense; let the lifting up of my hands be as the evening sacrifice.
3-4 Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips. * Do not incline my heart to any evil thing, 
to practice wicked deeds with men who work iniquity; and let me not eat of their delicacies. 
5 Let the righteous strike me; it shall be a kindness. And let him rebuke me; it shall be as oil for the head. Let my head not refuse it. For
6 my prayer is still against their calamities. * Their judges are thrown down by the sides of the rock, and they shall hear
7 my words, for they are pleasant. * As when one plows and breaks open the earth, our bones are scattered at the mouth of the abyss <note>original: "الهاوية" (al-hawiya) — the grave or the realm of the dead.</note>.
8-9 * But my eyes are toward You, O Lord God; in You I take refuge; do not leave my soul destitute. * Keep me
10 from the snare they have laid for me, and from the traps of the workers of iniquity. * Let the wicked fall into 
their own nets, while I escape altogether.

## Chapter Nine

<margin>1-2</margin> Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn out her seven pillars. * She has prepared her meat, she has mixed 
<margin>3</margin> her wine; she has also set her table. * She has sent out her maidens to call from the highest points of 
<margin>4-5</margin> the city: * "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks understanding, she says: * "Come, 
<margin>6</margin> eat of my bread and drink of the wine I have mixed. * Leave your simple ways and live, and walk in the way of understanding."
<margin>7</margin> He who corrects a mocker brings shame upon himself, and he who rebukes a wicked man brings a blemish upon himself.
<margin>8-9</margin> * Do not rebuke a mocker, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. * Give to a wise man, and he will become 
<margin>10</margin> even wiser; teach a righteous man, and he will increase in learning. * The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One 
<margin>11-12</margin> is understanding. * For by me your days shall be multiplied, and years of life shall be added to you. * If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; but if you mock, you alone will bear the burden.
<margin>13-14</margin> The foolish woman is clamorous; she is simple and knows nothing. * She sits at the door of her house, 
<margin>15</margin> on a seat in the high places of the city, * calling to those who pass by, who go straight on their paths:
<margin>16-17</margin> * "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" And to him who lacks understanding, she says: * "Stolen waters 
<margin>18</margin> are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is delicious." * But he does not know that the shadows <term>al-akhila: the spirits of the dead or phantoms</term> are there, and that her guests are in the depths of the underworld <term>al-hawiya: the abyss or the realm of the dead</term>.

## Chapter Ten

<margin>1-2</margin> The Proverbs of Solomon—A wise son makes a father glad, but a foolish son is the grief of his mother. * Treasures 
<margin>3</margin> of wickedness do not profit, but righteousness delivers from death. * The Lord does not let the soul of the righteous go hungry, 
<margin>4</margin> but He thwarts the desire of the wicked. * He who works with a slack hand becomes poor, but the hand of the diligent 
<margin>5</margin> makes rich. * He who gathers in summer is a wise son, and he who sleeps during harvest is a disgraceful 
<margin>6-7</margin> son <note>original: "ibn makhzan," literally "son of the storehouse," idiomatically used here for one who brings shame</note>. * Blessings are on the head of the righteous, but the mouth of the wicked covers violence <term>dhulm: typically meaning injustice or oppression</term>. * The memory of the righteous 
<margin>8</margin> is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot. * The wise in heart accepts commands, but the foolish of lips 
<margin>9</margin> will be cast down. * He who walks in integrity walks securely, but he who perverts his ways will be known

### Chapter Twenty-Four

<margin>1-2</margin> Do not envy people of evil, nor desire to be with them; * for their hearts meditate on violence <note>original: "الاغتصاب" (al-ightisab) – while used today for rape, in this context it refers to general extortion or seizing by force.</note> and their lips talk of trouble.

<margin>6-7</margin> * For by wise counsel you shall wage your war, and salvation is in a multitude of counselors. * Wisdom is too high 
<margin>8</margin> for a fool; he does not open his mouth in the gate <note>original: "الباب" (al-bab) – referring to the city gate, the historical site of judicial and social assembly.</note>. * He who plots to do evil will be called a mischief-maker. 
<margin>9</margin> * The thought of foolishness is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to men. * If you faint in the day 
<margin>10</margin> of adversity, your strength is small. * Deliver those who are being led to death, and those drawn toward slaughter. 
<margin>11</margin> Do not hold back. * If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not He who weighs hearts understand? And He who keeps 
<margin>12</margin> your soul, does He not know? And He will render to a man according to his work. 
<margin>13-14</margin> My son, eat honey because it is good, and the honeycomb is sweet to your palate. * So shall the knowledge of wisdom be for your soul; if you have found it, there shall be a reward, and your hope shall not be cut off. 
<margin>15</margin> * Do not lie in wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous. Do not plunder his home; * for the righteous man falls 
<margin>16</margin> seven times and rises again. But the wicked stumble into calamity. * Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not 
<margin>17</margin> your heart be glad when he stumbles, * lest the Lord see it and it be evil in His eyes, and He turn away 
<margin>18</margin> His wrath from him. * Do not fret because of evildoers, nor be envious of the wicked <note>original: "الائمة" (al-a'immah) – literally 'leaders' or 'imams,' used here to denote leaders of wickedness or the guilty.</note>; * for there will be no reward for the evil. 
<margin>21</margin> The lamp of the wicked will be put out. * My son, fear the Lord and the king. Do not associate with those given to change. 
<margin>22</margin> * For their calamity will rise suddenly, and who knows the ruin that both can bring?
