<margin>10</margin> Do not slander a servant to his master, lest he curse you and you be found guilty. * There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless
<margin>11</margin> its mother. * There is a generation pure in its own eyes, yet it has not been washed from its own filth. * There is a generation—how lofty are
<margin>12</margin> its eyes, and its eyebrows are lifted up! * There is a generation whose teeth are swords and its molars are knives, to devour
<margin>13</margin> the poor from off the earth and the needy from among men.
<margin>14</margin> <margin>15</margin> The leech has two daughters: "Give! Give!" There are three things that are never satisfied, four that do not say, "Enough": * The grave <note>original: "الهاوية" (al-hāwiyah) — the abyss or the realm of the dead</note>,
<margin>16</margin> the barren womb, the land that is not satisfied with water, and the fire that never says, "Enough."
<margin>17</margin> The eye that mocks a father and despises obedience to a mother—the ravens of the valley will pick it out and the young eagles will eat it.
<margin>18</margin> <margin>19</margin> Three things are too wonderful for me, and four I do not know: * The way of an eagle in the heavens, the way
<margin>20</margin> of a serpent on a rock, the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman. * Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eats and wipes her mouth and says, "I have done no wrong."
<margin>21</margin> <margin>22</margin> Under three things the earth trembles, and under four it cannot bear up: * Under a servant when he
<margin>23</margin> reigns, and a fool when he is full of bread; * under a hateful woman when she is married, and a maidservant when she succeeds <note>or inherits the position of</note> her mistress.
<margin>24</margin> <margin>25</margin> Four things are small on the earth, but they are exceedingly wise: * The ants are a people not strong,
<margin>26</margin> yet they prepare their food in the summer; * the rock badgers <term>rock badgers: <note>original: "الوبار" (al-wabār) — referring to the Syrian hyrax, a small mammal that lives in rocky terrain</note></term> are a weak folk, yet they make their homes in
<margin>27</margin> <margin>28</margin> the rock; * the locusts have no king, yet they all go out in ranks; * the spider <note>While the Arabic says "العنكبوت" (spider), some historical translations suggest a gecko or lizard</note> takes hold with her hands and is found in kings' palaces.
<margin>29</margin> Three things are stately in their stride, and four are comely in their gait: * The lion, which is mighty among beasts
<margin>30</margin> and does not turn back from any; * the one with lean flanks <note>original: "ضامر الشاكلة" (ḍāmir al-shākila) — likely referring to a greyhound or a strutting rooster</note>, the he-goat, and a king against whom there is no rising up.
<margin>31</margin> <margin>32</margin> If you have been foolish in exalting yourself, or if you have devised evil, put your hand on your mouth. * For the churning
<margin>33</margin> of milk brings forth butter <note>original: "جبناً" (jubnan) — literally "cheese," but in the context of "churning" (pressing) milk, it refers to the solid product like butter or curds</note>, and the wringing of the nose brings forth blood, and the churning of anger brings forth strife.

Proverbs * 31 *

### Chapter Thirty-One

<margin>1-2</margin> The words of Lemuel, king of Massa <note>original: "مسا" (Massa) — likely a reference to a North Arabian kingdom, though the word also means "oracle" or "burden"</note>, which his mother taught him: * "What, my son? And what, O son of my
<margin>3</margin> womb? And what, O son of my vows? — * Do not give your strength to women, nor your ways
<margin>4</margin> to that which destroys kings. * It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink
<margin>5</margin> wine, nor for princes to crave intoxicating drink <note>original: "المسكر" (al-muskir) — any strong fermented beverage</note>, * lest they drink and forget what is decreed, and pervert the justice <note>original: "حجة" (hujjah) — legal case or plea</note> of all the children of
<margin>6-7</margin> affliction. * Give intoxicating drink to him who is perishing, and wine to those of bitter soul. * Let him drink and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more.
<margin>8-9</margin> Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all orphans. * Open your mouth, judge
righteously, and defend the poor and the needy."
<margin>10</margin> A virtuous woman—who can find her? For her worth is far above pearls. * The heart of her husband trusts in her,
<margin>11</margin> so he will have no lack of gain <note>original: "غنيمة" (ghanimah) — spoils of war, used here to mean household profit or provision</note>. * She does him good and not evil all the days of her life. * She seeks wool
<margin>13</margin> and flax, and works with willing hands. * She is like the merchant ships; she brings her food from
<margin>15</margin> afar. * She also rises while it is yet night, and provides food for her household, and a portion <note>original: "فريضة" (faridah) — a prescribed duty or allotted meal</note> for her maidens. * She considers
<margin>17</margin> a field and buys it; from the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard. * She girds her loins with strength, and strengthens her arms.
<margin>18</margin> She perceives that her merchandise is good. Her lamp does not go out at night. * She stretches out her hands to the
<margin>20</margin> distaff <note>original: "المغزل" (al-mighzal) — the rod used in spinning</note>, and her hands hold the spindle. * She extends her hand to the poor, yes, she reaches out her hands to the
<margin>21</margin> needy. * She is not afraid of snow for her household, for all her household are clothed with scarlet garments <note>original: "حللاً" (hulalan) — fine robes or suits</note>.
<margin>22</margin> * She makes tapestry for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple. * Her husband is known in the
<margin>23</margin> gates, when he sits among the elders of the land. * She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies
<margin>25</margin> sashes for the merchant <note>original: "الكنعاني" (al-kan‘ani) — literally "Canaanite," a term synonymous with "merchant" in the ancient world</note>. * Strength and honor are her clothing; she shall rejoice in time to come. * She opens
<margin>27</margin> her mouth with wisdom, and on her tongue is the law of kindness. * She watches over the ways of her household, and does not eat
<margin>28</margin> the bread of idleness. * Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her: * "Many daughters
<margin>29</margin> have done virtuously, but you excel them all." * Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain.
<margin>30</margin>

# Ecclesiastes

## Chapter One

<margin>1-2</margin> The words of the Preacher <note>original: "الجامعة" (al-Jami'ah) — literally meaning 'The Assembler' or 'The Convener,' usually translated into English as 'The Preacher' or 'Qoheleth'</note>, the son of David, the king in Jerusalem. * Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher;
<margin>3</margin> vanity of vanities, all is vanity. * What profit has a man from all his labor in which
<margin>4</margin> he toils under the sun? * One generation passes away, and another generation comes, but the earth stands forever.
<margin>5-6</margin> The sun rises and the sun sets, and hurries to its place where it rises. * The wind
goes toward the south, and turns around to the north. It whirls around continually, and the wind returns to its circuits.
<margin>7</margin> All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full. To the place
<margin>8</margin> from which the rivers come, there they return again. * All words <note>original: "الكلام" (al-kalam) — can refer to 'speech' or 'things/matters'</note> fall short;
man cannot tell it all. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled
<margin>9</margin> with hearing. * That which has been is what will be, and that which was done is what will be done, for there is nothing
<margin>10</margin> new under the sun. * If anything is found of which it is said, "See, this is new," it has already
<margin>11</margin> been in the ages that were before us. * There is no remembrance of former things, and the later things also which
will be, there will be no remembrance of them among those who come after them.
<margin>12</margin> I, the Preacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem. * And I set my heart
to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under heaven. It is a grievous task <note>original: "عناء رديء" (ana' radi') — a difficult or evil toil</note>
that God has given to the sons of men to be exercised with. * I have seen all the works that are done under the
<margin>15</margin> sun, and behold, all is vanity and grasping for the wind <note>original: "قبض الريح" (qabd al-rih) — a metaphor for futility, like trying to catch the wind in one's hand</note>. * What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is
<margin>16</margin> lacking cannot be recovered. * I spoke with my heart, saying, "Behold, I have attained greatness and increased in wisdom
more than anyone who was before me over Jerusalem, and my heart has seen much wisdom and knowledge."

Solomon, David, Jerusalem, Vanity of vanities, The Sun, Wisdom, Chapter One

<summary>This page contains the opening of the Book of Ecclesiastes, where the author, identified as the son of David, reflects on the repetitive and seemingly futile nature of life and human effort. He concludes that all worldly pursuits are "vanity" and that there is nothing truly new under the sun.</summary>
<keywords>Ecclesiastes, Solomon, vanity of vanities, cycles of nature, futility, wisdom, Jerusalem, nothing new under the sun</keywords>

<margin>17</margin>...and knowledge. And I set my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. Then I perceived that
<margin>18</margin>this also is a grasping of the wind <note>original: "قبض الريح" (qabd al-rih) — a vivid metaphor for futility, like trying to catch or herd the wind</note>. For in much wisdom is much grief, and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow.

->Chapter Two<-

<margin>1</margin>I said in my heart, "Come now, I will test you with joy, that you may see what is good." And behold, this also is
<margin>2-3</margin>vanity. * Of laughter I said, "It is madness," and of joy, "What does it do?" * I searched in my heart how to gratify my flesh with wine, while my heart guided me with wisdom, and how to lay hold on folly, until I might see what is
<margin>4</margin>good for the sons of men to do under the heavens all the days of their lives. * I did great
<margin>5</margin>works. I built myself houses and planted myself vineyards. * I made for myself gardens
<margin>6</margin>and orchards <note>original: "فراديس" (faradees) — a word of Persian origin from which the English 'paradise' is derived, referring here to walled parks or pleasure gardens</note> and planted trees in them of every kind of fruit. * I made for myself pools of water
<margin>7</margin>to water the groves where trees grow. * I acquired male and female servants, and I had servants born in my house. I also had possessions of herds and flocks, more than all who were in
<margin>8</margin>Jerusalem before me. * I gathered for myself silver and gold and the treasures <note>original: "خصوصيات" (khususiyyat) — literally 'specialties' or 'peculiar treasures' belonging to rulers and provinces</note> of kings and provinces. I provided for myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men: a mistress
and mistresses <note>original: "سيدة وسيدات" (sayyidah wa-sayyidat) — literally 'a lady and ladies'; this is a famously difficult phrase in the Hebrew original (shiddah ve-shiddot) which this Arabic version interprets as noblewomen or concubines</note>. *
<margin>9</margin>So I became great and increased more than all who were before me in Jerusalem,
<margin>10</margin>and my wisdom also remained with me. * Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them. I did not withhold my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced in all my labor, and this was my reward
<margin>11</margin>for all my labor. * Then I looked on all the works that my hands had done and on the labor in which I had toiled; and indeed, all was vanity and a grasping of the wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
<margin>12</margin>Then I turned to look at wisdom and madness and folly. For what is the man who comes after the
<margin>13</margin>king who was appointed long ago? * Then I saw that wisdom has more profit than
<margin>14</margin>folly, as light has more profit than darkness. * The wise man's eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. And I also perceived that one event happens <note>The text implies that the same fate—death—eventually overtakes both the wise and the fool regardless of their choices</note>

<summary>In this passage, the Preacher recounts his experiments with pleasure, wealth, and grand architectural projects, concluding that despite their magnificence, they are ultimately empty. He reflects that while wisdom is superior to folly as light is to darkness, a single fate eventually befalls everyone.</summary>

But to the sinner He gives the task of gathering and heaping up, only to give to him who is good before God. This also is vanity and a grasping of the wind.

### Chapter Three

<margin>1-2</margin> For everything there is a season, and for every matter under the heavens a time: * A time for birth and a time for death;
<margin>3</margin> a time to plant and a time to uproot what is planted; * A time to kill and a time to heal;
<margin>4</margin> a time to tear down and a time to build; * A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn
<margin>5</margin> and a time to dance; * A time to scatter stones and a time to gather stones; a time to embrace

<margin>6</margin> a time, and a time to refrain from embracing; a time to gain and a time to lose.

<margin>8</margin> * and a time to speak; a time to love and a time to hate; a time for war and a time for peace.

<margin>11</margin> God has given to the sons of men to be occupied with. * He has made everything beautiful in its time. Also, He has put the world <note>original: "الدنيا" (al-dunya) — while this Arabic version uses a word meaning "the world" or "this life," the original Hebrew 'olam' is often translated as "eternity" in this context</note> in their hearts, so that no man can find out the work that God does from

<margin>18</margin> and for every work. * I said in my heart concerning the condition of the sons of men, that God

They all have one breath;
<margin>20</margin> man has no advantage over the beast, for all is vanity <note>original: "باطل" (baatil) — meaning empty, fleeting, or futile</note>. * All go
<margin>21</margin> to one place; all were from the dust, and to the dust all return. * Who knows the spirit of the sons of men, whether it goes upward, and the spirit of the beast, whether it goes
<margin>22</margin> downward to the earth? * So I saw that there is nothing better than that a man should rejoice in his works, for that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will happen after him?

<margin>9</margin> Two are better than one because they have a good reward for their labor.

## Chapter Five

<margin>1</margin> Guard your foot when you go to the house of God; for to draw near to listen is closer <note>meaning more acceptable or appropriate</note> than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not care that they do evil. 
<margin>2</margin> Do not be hasty with your mouth, and let not your heart be hurried to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth; therefore let your words be few. 
<margin>3</margin> For a dream comes through much business, and the voice of a fool from [much talk]...

<meta>This page continues the translation of the Book of Ecclesiastes (Al-Jami’ah), picking up in Chapter 5. The previous page discussed the benefits of companionship and the futility of isolated labor. Here, the Preacher moves into instructions regarding religious vows and further reflections on the vanity of wealth.</meta>

->Ecclesiastes * 5 * 6 *<-

<margin>4</margin> Too many words <note>The Arabic margin note 'كثرة الكلام' (abundance of words) serves as a thematic header for this section on caution in speech.</note>. When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, for He takes no pleasure in fools.
<margin>5-6</margin> Fulfill what you have vowed. It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it. Do not let your mouth lead your body into sin. And do not say before the messenger <note>original: "ملاك" (malak) — though this literally means 'angel,' it historically refers to a priest or temple official in this context</note> that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry 
<margin>7</margin> at your words and destroy the work of your hands? For this comes from an abundance of dreams and vanities and many words. But fear God. 
<margin>8</margin> If you see the oppression of the poor and the denial of right and justice in the land, do not be amazed by the matter. 
<margin>9</margin> For a high official is watched by one who is higher, and there are higher ones over them. And the profit of the land is for all; even the king
<margin>10</margin> is served by the field. He who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves 
<margin>11</margin> wealth with income. This also is vanity <note>original: "باطل" (baatil) — meaning emptiness, futility, or something without substance</note>. When goods increase, those who 
<margin>12</margin> eat them increase; and what profit is there to the owner except seeing them with his eyes? The sleep of the laborer is sweet, whether he eats 
<margin>13</margin> little or much, but the abundance of the rich man will not let him sleep. There is a grievous evil I have seen 
<margin>14</margin> under the sun: wealth kept for its owner to his hurt. And that wealth was lost through a bad 
<margin>15</margin> business; then he fathered a son, but there is nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother’s womb, naked shall he return, 
<margin>16</margin> going as he came, and he shall take nothing for his labor to carry away in his hand. And this also 
is a distressing misfortune. In every way as he came, so shall he go. What profit has he who has 
<margin>17</margin> labored for the wind? Also, he eats all his days in darkness and is greatly vexed, with sorrow and anger. 
<margin>18</margin> This is what I have seen to be good and fitting: for a person to eat and drink and find satisfaction in all the labor they perform under the sun during the days of their life 
<margin>19</margin> which God has given them, for this is their lot <term>lot: the Arabic 'نصيبه' (nasibuhu) refers to one's portion or destined share of life's experiences</term>. Also, every man to whom God has given wealth and riches and given him power over them, to eat from them and take his lot and rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God. 
<margin>20</margin> For he will not remember the days of his life much, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart.

### Chapter Seven

**1** A good name is better than precious oil, and the day of death is better than the day of birth. **2** Going to the house of mourning is better than going to the house of feasting, for that is the end of every man, and the living will lay it to heart. **3** Sorrow is better than laughter, for by the sadness of the face, the heart is made better. **4** The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. **5** It is better for a person to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools. **6** For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools. This also is vanity. **7** For oppression makes the wise man mad, and a gift <note>original: "العطية" (al-‘atiyya) — in this context, it implies a bribe or a corrupting influence</note> destroys the heart.

### Chapter Eight

**1** Who is like the wise man? And who understands the interpretation of a matter? A man’s wisdom brightens his face, and the hardness of his face is changed.
**2–3** I say: Observe the king’s command, and that because of the oath of God <term>oath of God: "yamin Allah" (يمين الله), a reference to a formal pledge of loyalty or a covenant made in the presence of the Divine</term>. Do not be in a hurry to leave his presence. Do not stand in a difficult <note>literally: "shāqq" (شاق), meaning arduous, distressing, or troublesome</note> matter, for he does whatever he pleases.
**4** For where the word of the king is, there is authority. And who can say to him, "What are you doing?"
**5–6** Whoever keeps the commandment will experience no harm, and the heart of the wise man knows the time and the judgment. For every matter has a time and a judgment, for the misery of man is great upon him.
**7** For he does not know what will be. For who can tell him how it will be?
**8** No man has authority over the spirit <term>spirit: "al-ruh" (الروح), which in this philosophical context also refers to the "breath of life"</term> to restrain the spirit, nor has he authority over the day of death. There is no discharge in war, nor will evil save its practitioners.
**9** All this I have seen as I applied my heart to every work done under the sun <note>original: "tahta al-shams" (تحت الشمس) — a central metaphor in this book for human life experienced on a purely material, earthly level</note> at a time when one man rules over another to his own hurt.
**10** And so I saw the wicked buried and gathered; and those who acted truthfully went from the holy place and were forgotten in the city. This also is vanity <note>original: "batil" (باطل) — meaning emptiness, futility, or something fleeting like a vapor</note>.
**11** Because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed quickly, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
**12** Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and his days are prolonged, yet I know that it will be well for those who fear God, who fear before Him.
**13** But it will not be well for the wicked, nor will he prolong his days like a shadow, because he does not fear before God.
**14** There is a vanity that occurs on the earth: that there are righteous men who are treated according to the deeds of the wicked, and there are wicked men who are treated according to the deeds of the righteous. I said that this also is vanity.
**15** So I praised joy, because there is nothing better for man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry, and this will remain with him in his labor during the days of his life which God gives him under the sun.

### Chapter Nine

**1** For all this I laid to my heart and explored all this: that the righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God. Man does not know whether it will be love or hatred; all is before them.
**2** All things come alike to all. One event happens to the righteous and the wicked, to the good, the pure, and the impure; to him who sacrifices and to him who does not sacrifice. As is the good man, so is the sinner; he who takes an oath is as he who fears an oath.
**3** This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: that one event happens to everyone. Moreover, the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that, they go to the dead.
**4** For who is excluded? For all the living there is hope, for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
**5** For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing at all; they have no further reward, for the memory of them is forgotten.
**6** Their love, their hatred, and their envy have already perished long ago; they no longer have a portion forever in anything that is performed under the sun.

**7** Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works.
**8** Let your garments be white at all times, and let not oil be lacking on your head <note>In the ancient Near East, white garments and scented oils were symbols of joy, celebration, and prosperity</note>.
**9** Enjoy life with the woman you love all the days of your vain life which He has given you under the sun—all the days of your vanity—for that is your portion in life and in your toil which you endure under the sun.
**10** Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might; for there is no work or thought or knowledge or wisdom in the Pit <term>the Pit: "al-hawiyah" (الهاوية), referring here to the realm of the dead, equivalent to the Hebrew "Sheol"</term> where you are going.
**11** I returned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle...

## Chapter Eleven

<margin>١-٢</margin> Cast your bread upon the face of the waters, for you will find it after many days. * Give a portion to seven, and also to eight, for you do not know what evil may come upon the earth.

### Chapter Twelve

1 Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years approach when you will say, "I find no pleasure in them." 
2 Before the sun and the light, the moon and the stars grow dark, and the clouds return after the rain; 
3 In the day when the keepers of the house tremble <note>Generally understood as the hands or arms of an aging person.</note>, and the strong men stoop <note>The legs.</note>, and the grinders cease because they are few <note>The teeth.</note>, and those looking through the windows grow dim <note>The eyes/eyesight.</note>; 
4 And the doors are shut in the street. When the sound of the grinding mill is low, and one rises up at the sound of a bird, and all the daughters of song are brought low <note>A poetic description of the loss of hearing or the weakening of the voice.</note>; 
5 Also, they are afraid of heights and of terrors in the way; and the almond tree blossoms <note>Likely referring to hair turning white.</note>, and the grasshopper becomes a burden, and desire fails; for man goes to his eternal home, and the mourners go about in the street; 
6 Before the silver cord is snapped, or the golden bowl is crushed, or the pitcher is broken at the spring, or the wheel is broken at the well <note>Metaphors for the cessation of life and the circulatory system.</note>; 
7 Then the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. 
8 "Vanity of vanities," says the Preacher <note>original: "Al-Jami'ah" (الجامعة), meaning the Assembler or Teacher</note>; "all is vanity."

9 Furthermore, because the Preacher was wise, he continued to teach the people knowledge; he weighed and searched out and set in order many proverbs. 
10 The Preacher sought to find words of delight, and words of truth written uprightly. 
11 The words of the wise are like goads <term>manasis: long sticks used to guide oxen</term>, and like well-driven nails are the words of the masters of assemblies, given by one Shepherd. 
12 And beyond these, my son, be warned: of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness to the flesh. 
13 Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. 
14 For God will bring every work into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether good or evil.

## Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

<margin>2</margin> Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth! For the Lord has spoken: "I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against Me."

<margin>3</margin> The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master’s crib; but Israel does not know, My people do not understand.

<margin>4</margin> Alas, sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a brood of evildoers, children who are corrupters! They have forsaken the Lord, they have provoked the <term>Holy One of Israel</term> <note>original: "quddūs Isrā’īl" — a characteristic title for God used throughout the Book of Isaiah.</note> to anger, they have turned away backward.

<margin>5</margin> Why should you be stricken again? You will revolt more and more. The whole head is sick and the whole heart faints.

<margin>6</margin> From the sole of the foot even to the head, there is no soundness in it, but wounds and bruises and fresh sores; they have not been closed or bound up, or soothed with oil.

<margin>7</margin> Your country is desolate, your cities are burned with fire; strangers devour your land in your presence; and it is desolate, as if overthrown by foreigners.

# Isaiah * 7 *

Damascus is Rezin, and within sixty-five years Ephraim <note>Ephraim was the largest tribe of the Northern Kingdom of Israel; here, the name represents the entire Northern Kingdom.</note> will be broken so that it is no longer a people. <margin>٩</margin> And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah <note>Referring to King Pekah of Israel.</note>. If you do not believe, you shall not be established. <note>This is a famous wordplay in the original Hebrew: "If you do not stand firm in faith, you will not stand at all."</note>

<margin>١٠</margin> Then the Lord spoke again to Ahaz, saying: <margin>١١</margin> "Ask for a sign for yourself from the Lord your God; <margin>١٢</margin> make your request deep or high above." <margin>٢٠</margin> In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor <note>The "hired razor" is a metaphor for the King of Assyria, whom God uses as a tool for judgment.</note> from across the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the legs, and it will remove the beard also. <note>In ancient Near Eastern culture, shaving a man's beard was a sign of extreme humiliation and defeat.</note>

<margin>٢٣</margin> And it shall happen in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines valued at a thousand pieces of silver will become a place for briers and thorns. <margin>٢٤</margin> With arrows and bows men will come there, because all the land will be briers and thorns. <margin>٢٥</margin> And as for all the mountains that were once hoed with a pickaxe, you will not go there for fear of briers and thorns; but they will become a place for oxen to roam and for sheep to trample."

### Chapter Eight

١ And the Lord said to me: "Take a large tablet for yourself and write on it with an ordinary pen <note>Literally "with a man’s pen," indicating the message should be clear and legible for everyone to read.</note> regarding **Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz** <note>original: "Mahīr Shalāl Ḥāsh Baz" (مهير شلال حاش بز). This Hebrew name means "Quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil," symbolizing how quickly Assyria would strip the wealth of Judah's enemies.</note>." ٢ And I took for myself faithful witnesses to record this: Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah. ٣ Then I approached the prophetess <note>Referring to Isaiah's wife, called a "prophetess" likely because of her husband's office or perhaps because she held a prophetic gift of her own.</note>, and she conceived and bore a son. Then the Lord said to me, "Call his name **Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz**; ٤ for before the child knows how to cry 'My father' and 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be carried away before the king of Assyria."

٥-٦ The Lord spoke to me again, saying: "Inasmuch as these people have refused the waters of Shiloah <note>The waters of Shiloah (or Siloam) flowed gently from a spring into Jerusalem, symbolizing God's quiet, steady protection, contrasted here with the violent 'river' of Assyria.</note> that flow softly, and rejoice in Rezin and the son of Remaliah; ٧ therefore, behold, the Lord is bringing up against them the waters of the River, strong and mighty—the king of Assyria and all his glory. He will rise over all his channels and go over all his banks. ٨ He will sweep into Judah, overflowing and passing through; he will reach even to the neck; and the spreading of his wings will fill the breadth of your land, O **Immanuel** <note>original: "‘Immānū’īl" (عمانوئيل) — "God is with us." Even in the midst of the "flood" of the Assyrian invasion, the land is still addressed as belonging to God's promised child.</note>."

٩ Be broken, O peoples, and be shattered! Give ear, all you distant parts of the earth. 1 O Lord, You are my God. I will exalt You; I will praise Your name, for You have done wonderful things.
2 Your purposes from of old are faithfulness and truth. * For You have turned a city into a heap of stones, a fortified village into a ruin; a palace of foreigners <note>original: "اعاجم" (A'ājim) — historically referring to non-Arabs, here translating the concept of hostile foreign powers</note> to be no city; it shall never be rebuilt.

10 Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; for ever and ever no one shall pass through it.
11 But the pelican and the hedgehog shall possess it; the crane and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch over it the line of ruin and the plummet <note>original: "مطمار" — a builder's tool used to ensure a straight line, here used metaphorically for a "measurement" of destruction.</note> of emptiness.

13 Thorns shall come up in its palaces, nettles and brambles in its fortresses. It shall be a habitation for jackals and an abode for ostriches.
14 And the wild beasts of the desert shall meet with the jackals, and the wild goat shall call to its companion; there the night-creature <note>original: "الليل" — often associated with the 'night hag' or 'screech owl' in prophetic imagery.</note> shall rest and find a place of repose for herself.
15 There the arrow-snake <term>Nakkaza: a species of desert snake known for leaping, though sometimes interpreted as a bird</term> shall nest and lay eggs, and hatch and gather them under her shadow. There also the falcons shall be gathered, each with its mate.

<margin>١٨</margin> the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloak. * According to their deeds, so He will repay:

<summary>This page describes a society where justice has collapsed, leading to a poetic confession of communal sin and blindness. In response to the lack of human leadership, God is depicted as a divine warrior who puts on the armor of righteousness to personally bring salvation and establish a new covenant.</summary>

<margin>1-2</margin> Arise, shine! For your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has dawned upon you. * For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness the nations. But upon you, the Lord will shine,

<margin>7</margin> gold and frankincense, and shall proclaim the praises of the Lord. * All the flocks of Kedar <note>A prominent nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert.</note> shall be gathered to you; the rams of 
<margin>8</margin> Nebaioth <note>Another nomadic people, often identified as the ancestors of the Nabataeans.</note> shall serve you. They shall go up with acceptance on My altar, and I will beautify My glorious house. * Who are 
<margin>9</margin> these who fly like a cloud, and like doves to their windows? * For the islands shall wait for Me, and the ships of

<margin>12</margin> the riches of the nations may be brought to you, with their kings led in procession. * For the nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish, 
<margin>13</margin> and those nations shall be utterly ruined. * The glory of Lebanon shall come to you—the cypress, the oak, and the box tree <note>original: "الشربين" (al-sharbin). Refers to various evergreen trees used for fine construction.</note>

<margin>1</margin> Who is this coming from Edom, with crimson-stained garments from Bozrah <note>original: "بصرة" (Bozrah), a major city in Edom. In biblical prophecy, Edom often represents the enemies of God’s people.</note>? This one who is majestic in his apparel,

### Chapter Sixty-Six

1 Thus says the Lord: The heavens are my throne, and the earth is my footstool. Where is the house that you would build for me, and where is the place of my rest?
2 * All these things my hand has made, and so all these things came to be, says the Lord. But this is the one to whom I will look: to the poor and the contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my word.
3 * He who slaughters a bull is as if he killed a man; he who slaughters a lamb is as if he broke a dog’s neck; he who offers a grain offering is as if he offered pig’s blood; he who burns frankincense is as if he blessed an idol. Indeed, they have chosen their own ways, and their souls delight in their abominations <note>original: "مكرهاتهم" (makruhatihim), referring to things that are detestable or ritually unclean.</note>.
4 * I also will choose their calamities <note>original: "مصائبهم" (masa'ibahum), often translated elsewhere as "delusions" or "follies."</note> and bring their fears upon them. Because I called and no one answered; I spoke and they did not hear; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight.
5 Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word: Your brothers who hated you and cast you out for my name’s sake said, "Let the Lord be glorified," so that he may appear to your joy; but they shall be put to shame.
6 * A sound of noise from the city! A voice from the temple! The voice of the Lord, repaying his enemies.

## Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> The words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin,

<margin>2</margin> * to whom the word of the Lord came in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, in the

<margin>3</margin> thirteenth year of his reign. * It also came in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the completion of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the exile of Jerusalem in the fifth month. <note>This introduction establishes the historical timeline, spanning about 40 years of ministry before the Babylonian captivity.</note>

<margin>4-5</margin> Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: * “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before

<margin>6</margin> you came out of the womb I sanctified you. I appointed you a prophet to the nations.” * Then I said, “Ah, Lord 

<margin>7</margin> God! <note>original: "يا سيد الرب" (Ya Sayyid al-Rabb) — This is a respectful address to the Sovereign Lord.</note> Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth.” * But the Lord said to me, “Do not say, ‘I am a youth,’ for

<margin>8</margin> you shall go to everyone I send you to, and whatever I command you, you shall speak. * Do not be afraid of

<margin>9</margin> their faces, for I am with you to deliver you,” says the Lord. * Then the Lord stretched out His hand and touched

<margin>10</margin> my mouth, and the Lord said to me: “Behold, I have put My words in your mouth. * See, I have appointed you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”

<margin>11</margin> Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying, “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And I said, “I

<margin>12</margin> see a branch of an almond tree.” <term>almond tree (shaked)</term> <note>In the original Hebrew, there is a wordplay here: 'almond' (shaked) sounds like the word for 'watching' (shoked). The vision means God is "watching" to see His word fulfilled.</note> * Then the Lord said to me, “You have seen well, for I am watching over My word

<margin>13</margin> to perform it.” * And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying, “What do you see?” And I said,

<margin>14</margin> “I see a boiling pot <note>literally: "a blown-upon pot," referring to a pot sitting on a fire being fanned.</note>, and its face is from the direction of the north.” * Then the Lord said to me, “From the north

<margin>15</margin> calamity <note>original: "الشر" (al-sharr) — evil or disaster.</note> shall break forth on all the inhabitants of the land. * For behold, I am calling all the families of the kingdoms of the north,” says the Lord. “They shall come and each one shall set his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem...”

### Chapter Two

<margin>1-2</margin> And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: * “Go and cry out in the ears of Jerusalem, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord: “I remember for you the devotion of your youth, the love of your betrothal, your following 
<margin>3</margin> after Me in the wilderness, in a land not sown.”’ * Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of His harvest. All who ate of it became guilty; evil came upon them,” says the Lord.
<margin>4-5</margin> Hear the word of the Lord, O house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. * Thus says the Lord: “What injustice did your fathers find in Me, that they went far from Me and followed 
<margin>6</margin> vanity <note>original: "الباطل" (al-batil) — often used in the Bible to refer to idols, implying they are empty, worthless, or breath-like.</note> and became vain themselves? * They did not say, ‘Where is the Lord who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and pits, through a land of drought and the shadow of 
<margin>7</margin> death <note>original: "ظل الموت" (zill al-mawt) — a famous poetic expression for extreme danger, darkness, or the realm of the dead.</note>, through a land that no man passed through and where no human dwelt?’ * And I brought you into a land of 
gardens to eat its fruit and its bounty. But you came and defiled My land and made My inheritance an abomination.
<margin>8</margin> * The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ and those who handle the Law <term>Law: the Torah, or religious instructions</term> did not know Me; the shepherds rebelled against Me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal <note>Baal was the primary Canaanite god of storms and fertility; his worship was the chief rival to the worship of Yahweh.</note> and went after things that do not profit.
<margin>9</margin> Therefore I will yet contend with you,” says the Lord, “and with your children's children I will contend. * For cross over to the islands of 
<margin>10</margin> Kittim <note>Kittim refers to Cyprus and the western regions, representing the western edge of the known world.</note> and see; send to Kedar <note>Kedar refers to the nomadic tribes of the Arabian desert, representing the eastern edge of the known world.</note> and observe very carefully and see if such a thing has ever happened.
<margin>11</margin> * Has a nation ever changed its gods, even though they are not gods? But My people have changed their glory for that which 
<margin>12</margin> does not profit. * Be astonished, O heavens, at this, and shudder; be utterly desolate,” says the Lord.

### Chapter Three

<margin>1</margin> It is said: "If a man divorces his wife, and she goes from him and becomes another man’s, may
he return to her again?" Would not that land be greatly polluted? But you have played the harlot
<margin>2</margin> with many lovers; yet return again to Me, says the Lord. * Lift up your eyes to
the desolate heights <note>original: "الهضاب" (al-hidab) — the high places where pagan rituals and illicit worship often took place.</note> and see: where have you not been violated? By the roads you have sat for them like an Arab <term>Arab: (اعرابي - a'rabi) here referring to a desert-dweller or nomad waiting in ambush.</term> in the
<margin>3</margin> wilderness; and you have polluted the land with your harlotries and your wickedness. * Therefore the showers have been withheld, and there has been no
<margin>4</margin> latter rain <note>The "latter rain" (the spring rains) was essential for the ripening of crops; its absence was viewed as a divine judgment.</note>. You have a harlot’s forehead; you refuse to be ashamed. * Will you not from
<margin>5</margin> this time cry to Me, "My Father, You are the guide of my youth"? * Will He remain angry forever? Will He keep
His grudge to the end? Behold, you have spoken and done evil things as much as you could.
<margin>6</margin> The Lord said also to me in the days of Josiah the king: "Have you seen what backsliding
Israel has done? She has gone up on every high mountain and under every green tree, and there played the harlot.
<margin>7</margin> * And I said, after she had done all these things, 'Return to Me.' But she did not return. And her treacherous sister Judah saw it."

٤ Lord. * Beware every one of his friend, and in no brother let you trust; for every brother acts as a **supplanter** <note>original: "يعقب عقباً"; a Hebrew wordplay on the name Jacob (Ya'qub), meaning one who trips up or takes the heel of another, indicating deep-seated treachery</note>, and every friend goes about in slander. *

٨ because of the daughter of my people? Their tongue is a deadly arrow; it speaks deceit. With his mouth one speaks peace to his friend,

desolation without inhabitant."
١٢ Who is the wise man who may understand this? And who is he to whom the mouth of the Lord has spoken, that he may declare it?

1 Thus says the Lord: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and there speak this word, 2 and say, 'Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David—you, your servants, and your people who enter through these gates! 3 Thus says the Lord: Execute right and justice, and deliver the one who has been robbed from the hand of the oppressor. Do no wrong and do no violence to the stranger, the orphan, or the widow, and do not shed innocent blood in this place. 4 For if you indeed do this thing, then kings sitting for David on his throne shall enter the gates of this house, riding in chariots and on horses—he, his servants, and his people. 5 But if you will not hear these words, I swear by Myself,' says the Lord, 'that this house shall become a ruin.'"

6 * For thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah: "You are like <term>Gilead</term> <note>A region east of the Jordan River famous for its lush forests and healing balms.</note> to Me, like the summit of <term>Lebanon</term> <note>Famed for its majestic cedar trees, which were used to build the royal palace in Jerusalem.</note>; yet I will surely make you a wilderness, like cities that are not inhabited. 7 I will set destroyers against you, every man with his weapons; they shall cut down your finest cedars and cast them into the fire. 8 And many nations will pass by this city, and each will say to his neighbor, 'Why has the Lord done such a thing to this great city?' 9 * Then they will answer, 'Because they have forsaken the covenant of the Lord their God, and worshiped other gods and served them.'"

10 Do not weep for the dead, nor lament him; weep bitterly for him who goes away <note>Referring to the exiled King Shallum (Jehoahaz), who was taken to Egypt.</note>, for he shall never return again to see [his native land].

## Chapter Twenty-Four

<margin>1</margin> The Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets of figs were set before the temple of the Lord, after Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "نبوخذراصر" (Nabūkhadrāṣar); the King of Babylon (r. 605–562 BCE) who conquered Jerusalem.</note> king of Babylon had carried away captive Jeconiah the son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the princes of Judah with the craftsmen <margin>2</margin> and the smiths from Jerusalem, and had brought them to Babylon. In one basket were very good figs, like the figs that are first-ripe <note>original: "التين الباكوري" (al-tīn al-bākūrī); the early figs of the season, considered a delicacy.</note>; and in the other basket were very bad figs, which could not be eaten because they were so <margin>3</margin> rotten. Then the Lord said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" And I said, "Figs: the good figs are very good, and the bad ones are very bad, so rotten they cannot be eaten."

<margin>4-5</margin> Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying: "Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: 'Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge the captives of Judah, whom I have sent out of this place into the land of the <margin>6</margin> Chaldeans <term>Chaldeans: "الكلدانيين" (al-Kaldāniyyīn); the people of southern Mesopotamia who ruled the Neo-Babylonian Empire.</term> for their own good. For I will set my eyes on them for good, and I will bring them back to this land.'"

### Chapter Twenty-Five

1 The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah in the fourth year of Jehoiakim <note>Jehoiakim was a son of Josiah and a king of Judah who reigned as a vassal to Egypt and then Babylon.</note>
2 son of Josiah, king of Judah (this was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "نبوخذراصر" (Nabūkhadrāṣar); the powerful King of Babylon who destroyed the First Temple.</note> king of Babylon), which Jeremiah the prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying:
3 "From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, even to this day—these twenty-three years—the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you early and often, but you have
4 not listened. And the Lord has sent to you all His servants the prophets, sending them early and often, but you have not listened,
5 nor inclined your ear to hear. They said, 'Return now every one of you from his evil way and from the wickedness of your deeds, and dwell in the land that the Lord has given to you and your fathers from of old
6 and forever. Do not go after other gods to serve them and worship them, and do not provoke me to anger with the work of your hands, so that I do no harm to you.'

8-9 "Therefore thus says the Lord of Hosts: 'Because you have not heard my words, behold, I will send and take all the families of the north,' says the Lord, 'and I will send to Nebuchadnezzar my servant, the king of Babylon, and will bring them against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all these nations 
10 all around. I will utterly destroy them, and make them an astonishment, a hissing, and a perpetual desolation. And I will take from them the voice...'" <note>The text concludes here mid-sentence, leading into the description of the silencing of joy and daily life in the following verses.</note>

## Chapter Twenty-Nine

1 These are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the remnant of the elders of the captivity, to the priests, the prophets, and all the people whom **Nebuchadnezzar** <note>The powerful King of the Neo-Babylonian Empire who conquered Jerusalem.</note> had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon. 
2 This was after King **Jeconiah** <note>Also known as Jehoiachin; he was the young king surrendered to Babylon.</note>, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the smiths had departed from Jerusalem. 
3 The letter was sent by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, whom **Zedekiah** <note>The final king of Judah, placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar.</note> king of Judah sent to Babylon, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, saying: 
4 "Thus says the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel, to all the captives whom I have caused to be carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: 
5-6 Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruit. * Take wives and beget sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons and give your daughters to husbands, so that they may bear sons and daughters. 
7 And increase there, and do not diminish. * And seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to the Lord for it; for in its peace you will have peace." <note>This was a radical command: Jeremiah tells the exiles to seek the prosperity of their enemy's city, Babylon, rather than praying for its immediate downfall.</note>
8 For thus says the Lord of Hosts, the God of Israel: "Do not let your prophets and your diviners who are in your midst deceive you, nor listen to your dreams which you cause to be dreamed. 
9 * For they prophesy falsely to you in My name; I have not sent them," says the Lord. 
10 For thus says the Lord: "When seventy years are completed for Babylon, I will visit you and perform My good word toward you, to bring you back to this place. <note>The 'seventy years' represents a full lifetime, signaling that the current generation of adults would likely not see the return themselves.</note>
11 For I know the thoughts that I think toward you," says the Lord, "thoughts of peace and not of evil, to give you a future and a hope. 
12 Then you will call upon Me and go and pray to Me, and I will listen to you. 
13 And you will seek Me and find Me, when you search for Me with all your heart. 
14 I will be found by you," says the Lord, "and I will bring you back from your captivity; I will gather you from all the nations and from all the places where I have driven you," says the Lord, "and I will bring you back to the place from which I caused you to be carried away captive."

## Jeremiah * 40 *

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord after <term>Nebuzaradan</term> <note>original: "رئيس الشرط" — literally "chief of the guard," referring to the captain of the Babylonian royal guard.</note>, the captain of the guard, released him from **Ramah** <note>A town about five miles north of Jerusalem, used as a transit point for captives being sent to Babylon.</note>. But you, gather wine, figs, and oil, and put them in your storage jars, and live in the cities you have taken over."

### Chapter Forty-One

**1** In the seventh month <note>Approximately October, two months after the fall of Jerusalem.</note>, **Ishmael** son of Nethaniah son of Elishama, who was of the royal family and one of the chief officers of the king, came with ten men to Gedaliah son of Ahikam at Mizpah. As they ate bread together there in Mizpah, **2** Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the ten men who were with him rose up and struck down **Gedaliah** son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, with the sword. Thus he killed the one whom the king of Babylon had appointed over the land.

**3** Ishmael also killed all the Jews who were with him—that is, with Gedaliah—at Mizpah, as well as the **Chaldean** <term>Chaldean</term> <note>Another term for the Babylonians, who were the ruling power of the time.</note> soldiers who were found there.

**4** On the second day after the killing of Gedaliah, while no one yet knew of it, **5** eighty men arrived from **Shechem**, **Shiloh**, and **Samaria** <note>Ancient cities in the northern kingdom of Israel.</note>. Their beards were shaved, their clothes were torn, and they had gashed themselves <note>original: "مخمّشين" — Ritual cutting of the skin, a sign of extreme mourning for the destroyed Temple, even though it was technically forbidden by Jewish law.</note>. When he met them, he said to them, "Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam." **7** But when they reached the middle of the city, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the men with him slaughtered them and threw them into a cistern.

## Chapter Forty-Four

<margin>1</margin> The word that came to **Jeremiah** <note>The prophet tasked with delivering God's messages during the fall of Judah.</note> concerning all the Jews dwelling in the land of

<margin>5</margin> the prophets, rising early and sending them, saying, 'Oh, do not do this abominable thing that I hate!' * But they did not listen

other gods in the land of Egypt where you have come to dwell, that you may be cut off and that you may become

Judah, the wickedness of their wives, your own wickedness, and the wickedness of your wives, which they committed in the land of Judah

and My statutes that I set before you and before your fathers."

# Chapter Forty-Six

<margin>1-2</margin> The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations: Concerning Egypt, concerning the army of Pharaoh Necho, king of Egypt, which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah:

<margin>3-4</margin> Prepare the buckler and the shield, and move forward to battle! Harness the horses and mount up, you <margin>5</margin> horsemen! Stand forth with your helmets; polish the spears, and put on the coats of mail. Why have I seen them dismayed and turned back? Their mighty ones are beaten down; they have fled in haste and do not look back. Terror <margin>6</margin> is all around, says the Lord. The swift cannot flee away, nor can the mighty man escape. In the north, <margin>7</margin> by the side of the river Euphrates, they have stumbled and fallen. Who is this that rises like the Nile, like rivers whose <margin>8</margin> waters toss? Egypt rises like the Nile, and like rivers its waters toss. He says, "I will rise up and cover the <margin>9</margin> earth; I will destroy the city and those who dwell in it." Advance, O horses! Drive furiously, O chariots! Let the mighty men come forth: <term>Cush</term> <note>Modern-day Ethiopia and Sudan</note> and <term>Put</term> <note>Likely modern Libya</note> who handle the shield, and the <term>Lydians</term> <note>North African allies or mercenaries</note> who handle <margin>10</margin> and bend the bow. For this day belongs to the Lord God of Hosts, a day of vengeance, to take vengeance on His adversaries. The sword shall devour and be satisfied, and shall drink its fill of their blood; for the Lord God of Hosts has a <margin>11</margin> sacrifice in the north country by the river Euphrates. Go up to Gilead and take <term>balm</term> <note>A medicinal resin famous for healing wounds</note>, O virgin daughter of Egypt! In <margin>12</margin> vain you use many medicines; there is no healing for you. The nations have heard of your shame, and your cry has filled the earth; for the mighty man has stumbled against the mighty, and they have both fallen together.

## Chapter Fifty-One

1 Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will stir up against **Babylon**, and against those who dwell in the midst of those who rise up against me, a destroying wind. * And I will send to Babylon winnowers <note>Workers who toss grain into the air so the wind blows away the useless husks (chaff)</note> who shall winnow her and empty her land; for 
3 they shall be against her on every side in the day of trouble. * Against him who bends his bow, let the archer draw, and against him who prides himself in his armor; do not spare her young men; but utterly destroy all her army. 
4-5 * Thus the slain shall fall in the land of the **Chaldeans**, and those thrust through in her streets. * For **Israel** and **Judah** <note>The northern and southern kingdoms of the Jewish people</note> have not been forsaken by their God, the Lord of Hosts, though their land was filled with sin against the **Holy One of Israel**. 
6 Flee from the midst of Babylon, and every man save his life! Do not be cut off in her iniquity; for this is the time of the Lord’s vengeance; He shall render to her a recompense. * Babylon was a golden cup in the Lord's hand, making all the earth drunk. The nations drank of her wine; for 
8 that reason the nations have gone mad. * Babylon has suddenly fallen and been destroyed. Wail for her! 
9 Take balm for her wound; perhaps she may be healed. * We would have healed Babylon, but she is not healed. Forsake her, and let us go 
10 every one to his own country; for her judgment reaches to the heavens and is lifted up even to the clouds. * The Lord has brought forth our righteousness <note>Meaning our vindication or the justice of our cause</note>. Come, and let us declare in **Zion** <note>The hill in Jerusalem where God was said to dwell among His people</note> the work of the Lord our God. 
11 Sharpen the arrows! Prepare the shields! The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the **Medes** <note>An ancient Iranian people who were key allies in the conquest of Babylon</note>; for His purpose is against Babylon to destroy it, because it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance for His temple. 
12 Set up the standard <note>A military banner or flag</note> upon the walls of Babylon! Strengthen the watch! Set up the watchmen! Prepare the ambush! For the Lord has both purposed and performed what He spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon. 
13 O you who dwell upon many waters <note>A reference to the network of canals and the Euphrates river that protected Babylon</note>, rich in treasures, 
14 your end has come, the measure of your greed. * The Lord of Hosts has sworn by Himself: "Surely I will fill you with men, as with locusts <note>original: "al-gawgha," referring to a swarming, noisy multitude</note>, and they shall lift up a shout against you."

# Lamentations of Jeremiah
## Chapter One

١ How lonely sits the city that was once full of people! How like a widow she has become, she who was great among the nations! The princess among the provinces <note>original: "السيدة في البلدان" (al-sayyida fi al-buldan). This reflects Jerusalem's former status as a regional power and cultural center.</note> has become a forced laborer.
٢ She weeps bitterly in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks. Among all her lovers <note>In the prophetic tradition, "lovers" usually refers to the political allies (like Egypt or Edom) that Jerusalem relied on instead of God.</note> there is none to comfort her. All her friends have dealt treacherously with her; they have become her enemies.
٣ Judah has gone into exile <note>original: "سبيت" (subiyat), referring to the forced deportation to Babylon.</note> because of affliction and great servitude. She dwells among the nations; she finds no rest. All her pursuers have overtaken her in the midst of her distress.
٤ The roads to Zion <note>Zion is the name of the hill on which the Temple stood, often used to represent the whole city of Jerusalem.</note> mourn because none come to the appointed feasts. All her gates are desolate;
٥ her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness. Her foes have become the head; her enemies prosper, for the Lord has afflicted her for the multitude of her transgressions. Her children have gone into captivity before the enemy.
٦ From the daughter of Zion <note>A poetic personification of the city and its people.</note> all her splendor has departed. Her princes have become like deer that find no pasture; they fled without strength before the pursuer.
٧ Jerusalem remembers in the days of her affliction and her wandering all the precious things she had from the days of old. When her people fell into the hand of the foe and there was no one to help her, the enemies saw her and laughed at her downfall.
٨ Jerusalem has sinned grievously; therefore she has become an uncleanness. All who honored her despise her because they have seen her nakedness; she herself also sighs and turns away.

> <margin>1</margin> How the gold has grown dim! How the fine gold <note>original: "الابريز" (al-ibriz); refers to the purest, most refined gold.</note> has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at

> they are now regarded as earthen jars, the work of a potter's hands!

### Chapter Two

1 And in the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar dreamed dreams; his spirit was troubled and his sleep left him. * 
2 Then the king commanded that the <term>magicians</term> <note>original: "al-majus"; a term referring to those practicing astrology or sacred rites</note>, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the <term>Chaldeans</term> <note>original: "al-kaldaniyyun"; an ethnic group in Babylonia famous for their study of the stars and divination</note> be summoned to tell the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king. * 
3 And the king said to them, "I have had a dream, and my spirit is troubled to know the dream." * 
4 Then the Chaldeans spoke to the king in <term>Aramaic</term> <note>original: "bi-al-aramiyya"; this marks a historical linguistic shift where the biblical text itself changes from Hebrew to Aramaic from this point forward</note>: "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will reveal its interpretation." * 
5 The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, "The word has gone out from me: if you do not make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall be cut into pieces, and your houses shall be made a dunghill. * 
6 But if you reveal the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts, rewards, and great honor. Therefore, reveal to me the dream and its interpretation." * 
7 They answered a second time and said, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will reveal its interpretation." * 
8 The king answered and said, "I know for certain that you are trying to gain time, because you see that the word has gone out from me— * 
9 that if you do not make known to me the dream, there is but one decree for you. For you have agreed on lying and corrupt words to speak before me until the time changes. Therefore, tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can reveal its interpretation to me." *

## Chapter Five

The inhabitants of Samaria fear for the calf of Beth-aven <note>original: "بيت آون" (Beth-Aven), meaning "House of Iniquity." This is a derogatory play on the name "Bethel" (House of God), where the golden calf was worshiped.</note>. Its people mourn over it, and its priests tremble for it, for its glory, because it has departed from it. 
**٦** It shall also be carried to Assyria as a tribute to the Great King. Ephraim shall be seized with shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of its own counsel. 
**٧** Samaria’s king shall perish like foam <note>original: "غثاء" (ghutha'), meaning foam, scum, or floating debris brought by a flood, symbolizing helplessness and rapid disappearance.</note> on the surface of the water. 
**٨** The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed. Thorns and thistles shall grow up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us,” and to the hills, “Fall on us!”
**٩** Since the days of Gibeah <note>A reference to a notorious crime of sexual violence and civil war found in the Book of Judges, used here as a benchmark for Israel's long history of corruption.</note>, you have sinned, O Israel. There they stood; did not the battle in Gibeah against the children of iniquity overtake them? 
**١٠** When I desire, I will discipline them; and peoples shall be gathered against them when they are bound for their double iniquity. 
**١١** Ephraim is a trained heifer that loves to thresh, but I will pass over her fair neck. I will harness Ephraim; Judah must plow; Jacob must harrow for himself.
**١٢** Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap according to mercy. Break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the Lord, until He comes and rains <note>original: "يعلمكم" (yu'allimukum), literally "teaches you," though in some biblical contexts this carries the sense of "raining" righteousness.</note> righteousness upon you. 
**١٣** You have plowed wickedness; you have reaped iniquity. You have eaten the fruit of lies because you trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your mighty men. 
**١٤** Therefore a tumult shall arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be destroyed, as Shalman <note>Likely referring to the Assyrian king Shalmaneser or a Moabite king named Shalman who destroyed this city.</note> destroyed Beth-arbel on the day of battle; the mother was dashed in pieces with her children. 
**١٥** Thus Bethel shall do to you because of your great wickedness. At dawn the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off.

## Chapter Eleven

**١-٢** When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son. The more they <note>original: "دعوهُم" (they called them), referring to the prophets calling the people.</note> called them, the more they went away from them; they kept sacrificing to the Baals <note>original: "البعليم" (al-Ba'alim), the plural form of Baal, local Canaanite deities.</note> and burning incense to carved images. 
**٣** And it was I who taught Ephraim to walk, taking them by their arms; but they did not know that I healed them. 
**٤** I led them with cords of human kindness, with ties of love. I was to them like those who lift the yoke from their necks, and I bent down to feed them.
**٥-٦** They shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Assyria shall be their king, because they refused to return to Me. The sword shall rage in their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them because of their own counsels. 
**٧** My people are bent on turning away from Me. Though they are called to the Most High, no one at all exalts Him. 
**٨** How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I set you like Zeboiim? <note>Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah, representing total and irreversible divine judgment.</note> My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.

## Chapter Twelve

<margin>1</margin> Ephraim herds the wind and pursues the east wind <note>The "east wind" (sirocco) is a dry, scorching desert wind, symbolizing destructive and worthless pursuits.</note>. Every day he multiplies lies and violence; they make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried to Egypt <note>A reference to Israel’s desperate and contradictory political alliances with rival superpowers.</note>. The Lord also has a dispute with Judah, and is set to punish Jacob according to his ways; according to his deeds He will repay him.

<margin>3-4</margin> In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his strength he struggled with God. He struggled with the Angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor. He found Him at Bethel, and there He spoke with us—even the Lord God of Hosts; <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The specific, personal name of God (Yahweh), emphasizing His eternal nature and covenant relationship.</note> is His name. So you, return to your God; observe mercy and justice, and wait on your God continually.

<margin>7-8</margin> Like a <term>Canaanite</term> <note>original: "الكنعاني" (al-Kan'ani). In the language of the time, this word became synonymous with "merchant" or "trader," here implying someone who uses dishonest scales.</note>, in his hand are scales of deceit; he loves to oppress. Ephraim said, "Indeed, I have become rich; I have found wealth for myself. In all my labors they shall find no iniquity in me that is sin." "But I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed festival. I have also spoken by the prophets, and multiplied visions; I have given parables by the hand of the prophets."

<margin>11 *</margin> Is there iniquity in Gilead? They are surely vanity. In Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; indeed, their altars are like heaps of stones in the furrows of the field.

<margin>12</margin> Jacob fled to the country of Aram; Israel <note>Jacob was renamed "Israel" after wrestling with the angel; the prophet uses both names to connect the people's history to their current state.</note> served for a wife, and for a wife...

## Chapter Thirteen

<margin>1-2</margin> When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel; but when he sinned with Baal, he died. <note>Baal was a Canaanite deity; the text suggests that turning to idolatry was the spiritual death of the nation.</note> * And now they sin more and more, and make for themselves molten images of their silver—idols according to their own understanding, all of it the work of craftsmen. They say of them, "Let those who sacrifice men kiss the calves!" <note>The "calves" refer to the golden statues established at Bethel and Dan as rival worship sites to Jerusalem.</note>
<margin>3</margin> * Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud and as the early dew that passes away; as the chaff that is blown from the threshing floor, and as smoke from a window. <note>These four metaphors—clouds, dew, chaff, and smoke—all emphasize the fleeting and temporary nature of a nation that abandons God.</note>
<margin>4</margin> Yet I am the Lord your God from the land of Egypt; and you shall know no god but me, for there is no savior 
<margin>5-6 beside me</margin> * I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of great thirst. * When they pastured, they were filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted; therefore they have forgotten me.
<margin>7-8</margin> Therefore I will be to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk by the way. * I will encounter them like a bear bereaved of her cubs, and I will tear open the ribcage of their heart; there I will devour them like a lioness, and the wild beast shall tear them.
<margin>9</margin> Your destruction, O Israel, is because you are against me, against your help. * Where is your king now, that he may save you

<margin>13</margin> unwise son, for he does not present himself at the proper time in the opening of the womb.
<margin>14</margin> From the power of the Grave <note>original: "الهاوية" (al-hawiya), referring to Sheol, the realm of the dead.</note> I will ransom them; from death I will redeem them. Where are your plagues, O death? Where is your sting, O Grave? Compassion shall be hidden from my eyes.

### Chapter Fourteen

<margin>1-2</margin> Return, O Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity. * Take words with you and return to the Lord. Say to Him: "Take away all iniquity and receive us graciously, so we may offer the sacrifice of our <margin>3</margin> lips." <note>Literally "the fruit of our lips," referring to prayer and praise as a substitute for animal sacrifice.</note> * Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses, nor will we say any more to the work of our hands, "You are our gods." <margin>4-5</margin> I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him. * I will be to Israel <margin>6</margin> like the dew; he shall blossom like the lily and strike his roots like Lebanon. <note>The cedars of Lebanon were famous in antiquity for their strength and deep roots.</note> * His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be <margin>7</margin> like the olive tree, and his fragrance like Lebanon. * Those who dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive like grain and blossom like a vine. <margin>8</margin> Their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon. * Ephraim shall say: "What have I to do anymore with idols?" I have answered and observed him. I am like a green cypress tree; from Me your fruit is found. <margin>9</margin> Who is wise that he may understand these things? Who is discerning that he may know them? For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous walk in them; but the transgressors stumble in them.

١١ "I am a hero." * Hurry and come, all you nations from every side, and gather yourselves. There,
١٢ O Lord, bring down Your heroes. * Let the nations be roused and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat <note>original: "وادي يهوشافاط" — literally meaning "The Lord Judges."</note>, for there I will
١٣ sit to judge all the nations from every side. * Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the winepress is full. The vats overflow, for

١٤ Multitudes, multitudes in the Valley of Decision <note>original: "وادي القضاء" — the place of final divine judgment.</note>, for the day of the Lord is near in the Valley of Decision.
١٥ * The sun and the moon grow dark, and the stars withdraw their brightness. * And the Lord roars from Zion,
١٦ and from Jerusalem He utters His voice, and the heavens and the earth tremble. But the Lord is a refuge for His people
١٧ and a stronghold for the children of Israel. * So you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, My holy mountain. And Jerusalem shall be holy, and foreigners shall never pass through it again.
١٨ And it shall come to pass on that day that the mountains shall drip with sweet wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the springs of Judah shall flow with water; and a fountain shall come forth from the house of the Lord and water the Valley of Shittim <note>original: "وادي السنط" — the Valley of the Acacias, representing an arid place made fertile by God’s presence.</note>.
١٩ * Egypt shall become a desolation and Edom shall become a desolate wilderness because of the violence done to the children of Judah, for they
٢٠ shed innocent blood in their land. * But Judah shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation
٢١ to generation. * And I will cleanse <note>original: "وابرى" — to acquit or declare innocent; refers to God settling the accounts of bloodguilt.</note> their blood which I have not yet cleansed, for the Lord dwells in Zion.
