# Amos
## Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds from Tekoa <note>original: "تقوع" — a small town in the wilderness of Judah, south of Jerusalem.</note>, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
<margin>2</margin> And he said: "The Lord roars from Zion and utters His voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the top of Carmel withers."
<margin>3</margin> Thus says the Lord: "For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment <note>original: "لا ارجع عنهُ" — literally "I will not return from it," a formulaic expression meaning the judgment is final and irrevocable.</note>;
<margin>4</margin> because they have threshed Gilead with threshing sledges <term>threshing sledges: heavy wooden frames with sharp iron teeth or stones underneath, used to crush stalks and separate grain</term> of iron. * So I will send a fire upon the house of Hazael,
<margin>5</margin> and it shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad <note>Hazael and Ben-hadad were successive kings of Aram (ancient Syria) known for their military campaigns against Israel.</note>. * And I will break the gate-bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitant from the Valley of Aven <note>original: "بقعة آون" — "Aven" means "wickedness" or "vanity"; this likely refers to a valley near Damascus noted for its idol worship.</note>, and the one who holds the scepter from Beth-eden; and the people of Aram shall go into captivity to Kir," says the Lord.
<margin>6</margin> Thus says the Lord: "For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment; because they
<margin>7</margin> carried away a whole captivity <note>meaning they captured entire populations, sparing no one, to sell them as slaves.</note> to deliver them up to Edom. * So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza, and it shall devour
<margin>8</margin> its palaces. * And I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and the one who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; and I will turn My hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish," says the Lord GOD.
<margin>9</margin> Thus says the Lord: "For three transgressions of Tyre, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment; because they
<margin>10</margin> delivered up a whole captivity to Edom, and did not remember the covenant of brotherhood <note>Refers to the historical treaty and friendly "brotherly" relations between the Phoenicians of Tyre and the Israelites under David and Solomon.</note>. * So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its palaces."
<margin>11</margin> Thus says the Lord: "For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment; because he pursued his brother with the sword, and stifled his compassion <note>original: "افسد مراحمهُ" — literally "corrupted his mercies," indicating that he destroyed his own natural feelings of pity.</note>, and his anger tore perpetually, and he kept his wrath
<margin>12</margin> forever. * So I will send a fire upon Teman, and it shall devour the palaces of Bozrah."
<margin>13</margin> Thus says the Lord: "For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment..."

## Chapter Three

<margin>1</margin> Hear this word that the Lord has spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole 
<margin>2</margin> family <note>original: "القبيلة" — literally 'tribe' or 'clan', but here referring to the entire nation of Israel as a single family unit.</note> that I brought up from the land of Egypt, saying: * "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities."

<margin>3-4</margin> Do two walk together unless they have made an appointment? * Does a lion roar in the thicket when he has no prey? Does a young lion cry out from his den if he has caught nothing? * Does 
<margin>5</margin> a bird fall into a snare on the earth when there is no trap for it? Does a snare spring up from the earth when it has 
<margin>6</margin> captured nothing at all? * Or is a trumpet blown in a city and the people do not tremble? Does 
<margin>7</margin> disaster occur in a city and the Lord has not caused it? * Surely the Lord God does nothing without revealing 
<margin>8</margin> His secret <note>original: "سره" — refers to God's divine counsel or private plans.</note> to His servants the prophets. * The lion has roared—who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken—who can but prophesy?

<margin>9</margin> Proclaim to the palaces in Ashdod and to the palaces in the land of Egypt, and say: "Assemble yourselves on the mountains of Samaria, and see the great unrest in her midst and the oppressions within her." 
<margin>10</margin> * "For they do not know how to do what is right," says the Lord, "those who store up 
<margin>11</margin> violence and robbery in their palaces." * Therefore thus says the Lord God: "An adversary shall surround the land; he shall strip your strength from you, and your palaces shall be plundered."

<margin>12</margin> Thus says the Lord: "As the shepherd rescues from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued who dwell in Samaria—in the corner of a bed and on the damask <note>original: "دمقس" — referring to fine, luxurious silk fabric or cushions, likely imported from Damascus.</note> of a couch." 
<margin>13</margin> * "Hear and testify against the house of Jacob," says the Lord God, the God of hosts, 
<margin>14</margin> * "that on the day I punish Israel for his transgressions, I will also punish the altars of Bethel; then the 
<term>horns of the altar<gloss>The four projections at the corners of the altar, considered its most sacred points and a place of asylum.</gloss></term> shall be cut off and fall to the ground. 
<margin>15</margin> * I will strike the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory <note>referring to houses inlaid with expensive ivory panels, a sign of extreme decadence.</note> shall perish, and the great houses shall come to an end," says the Lord.

<summary>Amos argues that Israel's unique relationship with God brings greater accountability, using a series of cause-and-effect questions to justify his prophetic warnings. The text concludes with a prophecy of total destruction for the wealthy elite of Samaria and the religious altars at Bethel.</summary>

## Chapter Four

Hear this word, you cows of Bashan <note>Bashan was a region east of the Jordan River famous for its lush pastures and well-fed livestock; here, the prophet uses it to satirize the wealthy, indulgent women of the capital.</note> who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress
<margin>2</margin> the poor and crush the needy, saying to their masters <note>original: "لسادتها" — referring to their husbands.</note>, "Bring us something to drink!" * The Lord God has sworn by His holiness: Behold, the days are coming upon you when they shall take you away with hooks, and your descendants with 
<margin>3</margin> fishhooks. * And you shall go out through the breaches in the wall, every woman straight ahead, and you shall be cast out toward the fortress <note>original: "الحصن" — likely referring to Harmon or a place of exile.</note>, says the Lord.
<margin>4</margin> Come to Bethel and transgress; to Gilgal and multiply transgression! Bring your 
<margin>5</margin> sacrifices every morning, and your tithes every three days. * Burn a thank-offering of leavened bread <note>Under Mosaic Law, leavened bread was generally forbidden on the altar; Amos is likely mocking their self-styled religious zeal.</note>, proclaim freewill offerings and announce them; for so you love to do, O children of Israel! says the Lord God.
<margin>6</margin> And I also gave you cleanliness of teeth <note>A poetic idiom for famine; there was no food to get the teeth dirty.</note> in all your cities, and lack of bread in all 
<margin>7</margin> your places; yet you have not returned to Me, says the Lord. * I also withheld the rain from you when there were still three months to the harvest. I made it rain on one city and I withheld rain from another city.
<margin>8</margin> One field was rained upon, and the field on which it did not rain withered. * So two or three cities wandered to one city to drink water, but they were not satisfied; yet you have not returned to Me, 
<margin>9</margin> says the Lord. * I struck you with blight and mildew. The locust <note>original: "القمص" — refers to a stage of the locust's growth or a specific type of crawling insect that devours crops.</note> frequently devoured your gardens, your vineyards, your fig trees, and your olive trees; yet you have not returned to Me, says the Lord.
<margin>10</margin> I sent among you a plague after the manner of Egypt. I killed your young men with the sword, along with your captured horses; I made the stench of your camps rise 
<margin>11</margin> even into your nostrils; yet you have not returned to Me, says the Lord. * I overthrew some of you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you were like a brand plucked from the burning; yet you have not returned to Me, 
says the Lord.
<margin>12</margin> Therefore thus will I do to you, O Israel! Because I will do this to you, 
<margin>13</margin> prepare to meet your God, O Israel! * For behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what his thought is; who makes the morning darkness and treads on the high places of the earth—Yahweh <note>original: "يهوه" — the personal, sacred name of God, often translated as 'The Lord'.</note>, the God of Hosts, is His name.

<summary>Amos rebukes the wealthy elite of Samaria for their cruelty and empty religious rituals, listing several natural disasters sent by God as warnings that the nation has failed to heed. It concludes with a powerful call for Israel to prepare for a direct encounter with their Creator.</summary>

## Chapter Five

1 Hear this word which I take up against you as a lamentation <note>original: "مرثاةً" — a funeral dirge; Amos is singing a funeral song for a nation that is still alive but spiritually dead.</note>, O house of Israel:
2 * The virgin of Israel has fallen; she shall rise no more. She lies forsaken on her land; there is no
3 one to raise her up. * For thus says the Lord God: The city that goes out by a thousand shall have a hundred left,
and that which goes out by a hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel.
4-5 For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek Me and live; * but do not seek Bethel <note>Bethel was a major cultic center; the name means "House of God," but Amos elsewhere calls it "House of Wickedness."</note>, 
nor enter Gilgal, nor pass over to Beersheba. For Gilgal shall surely go into captivity
6 and Bethel shall come to nothing. * Seek the Lord and live, lest He break out like a fire upon the house of Joseph <note>The "house of Joseph" refers to the Northern Kingdom, particularly the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.</note> 
7 and consume it, with no one in Bethel to quench it. * O you who turn justice
into wormwood <note>term: "افسنتيناً" (wormwood) — a plant known for its extreme bitterness, used here to describe how the elite have made the legal system bitter for the poor.</note> and cast righteousness down to the earth!
8 He who made the Pleiades and Orion <note>original: "الثريا والجبار" — The Seven Stars and the Giant; Amos highlights God’s power over the stars to contrast with the idols the Israelites were worshiping.</note>, and turns the shadow of death into morning and darkens the day into night;
9 who calls for the waters of the sea and pours them out on the face of the earth—the Lord <note>original: "يهوه" (Yahweh)</note> is His name. * He who brings
10 destruction upon the strong, so that destruction comes upon the fortress. * They hate
11 the one who rebukes in the gate <note>The "gate" of a city was the site of the marketplace and the law courts where elders sat in judgment.</note> and they abhor the one who speaks uprightly. * Therefore, because you tread down the poor
and take from him a tax of grain, you have built houses of hewn stone <note>Stone houses were an expensive luxury compared to the common mud-brick dwellings of the era.</note>, but you shall not dwell in them;
12 you have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine. * For I know your manifold transgressions
and your mighty sins, you who afflict the just and take bribes, turning aside the needy in
13 the gate. * Therefore the prudent keep silent in that time, for it is an evil time.
14 Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as
15 you have spoken. * Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the gate; it may be that the Lord God of hosts
will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.
16 Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Lord: In all the streets there shall be wailing,
and in all the highways they shall say, "Alas! Alas!" They shall call the farmer to mourning and those skilled
17 in lamentation to wailing. * In all vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through your midst, says the Lord.

## Chapter Seven

<margin>1</margin> Thus the Lord God showed me: behold, He was forming locusts at the beginning of the late crop's growth.
<margin>2</margin> It was the late crop after the king’s mowings. <note>The "king's mowing" was a tax or tribute of the first harvest; the "late crop" was what the people relied on for their own survival.</note> And it happened, when they had finished eating the grass of the land, that I said: "O Lord God, forgive, I pray! <margin>5</margin> the great deep and devoured the land. Then I said: "O Lord God, cease, I pray! How
<margin>6</margin> can Jacob stand? For he is small." So the Lord relented concerning this. "This also shall not be," said the Lord God.
<margin>7-8</margin> Thus He showed me: behold, the Lord was standing on a vertical wall, and in His hand was a plumb line <note>term: "زيج" (Zij) — usually refers to astronomical tables in later Arabic, but here it denotes a builder's tool used to check if a wall is perfectly straight.</note>. <margin>9</margin> in the midst of My people Israel. I will never pass by them again. The high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste, and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."

<margin>12</margin> from their own land.'" Then Amaziah said to Amos: "O seer, go, flee to the land of Judah!

### Chapter Eight

<margin>1-2</margin> Thus the Lord God showed me: behold, a basket for the harvest. <note>In the original Hebrew, this vision contains a pun between 'summer fruit' and 'the end.' <margin>4-5</margin> Hear this, you who trample the needy to destroy the poor of the land, saying: "When will the New Moon be over, that we may sell grain? <margin>6</margin> and making the <term>shekel<note>A unit of weight used for currency; by making it 'heavy,' the merchants cheated buyers out of more silver.</note></term> large, and falsifying the scales of deceit? That we may buy the weak for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of the wheat?"
<margin>7</margin> The Lord has sworn by the pride of Jacob: "I will never forget any of their deeds.

### Chapter Nine

<margin>8</margin> Israel from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir? * Behold, the eyes of the Lord God are on the sinful kingdom, and I will destroy it from the face of the earth; except that I will not

<margin>10</margin> among all nations, as grain is shaken in a sieve, yet not the smallest pebble shall fall to the ground. * All the sinners of My people shall die by the sword, who say, 'Evil shall not overtake or meet us.'
<margin>11</margin> In that day I will raise up the fallen <term>booth of David</term> <note>original: "مظلة داود" — referring to the restoration of the Davidic dynasty and the unity of the kingdom.</note> and wall up its breaches; I will raise up its ruins."

<margin>4</margin> * Though you exalt yourself like the eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I will

<margin>6</margin> would they not have stolen only till they had enough? <margin>9</margin> Esau? * Then your mighty men, O <term>Teman</term> <note>original: "تيمان" — a key city or district in Edom, famous in the ancient world for its 'wise men.'</note>, shall be dismayed, to the end that everyone from the mountains of Esau may be cut off by slaughter.
<margin>10</margin> * For violence against your brother <term>Jacob</term> <note>original: "يعقوب" — the ancestor of the Israelites; the text highlights the fraternal betrayal between the two nations.</note>, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever.
<margin>11</margin> * In the day that you stood on the other side—in the day that strangers carried captive his forces, when foreigners entered his gates and cast
<margin>12</margin> lots for Jerusalem—even you were as one of them. * But you should not have gazed on the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune..."

<margin>2</margin> Hear, all you peoples! Listen, O earth and all that is in it! Let the Lord God be a witness against you, the Lord from His holy temple.
<margin>3</margin> For behold, the Lord is coming out of His place; He will come down and walk upon the high places of the earth.
<margin>4</margin> The mountains will melt under Him, and the valleys will split like wax before the fire, like water poured down a steep slope.
<margin>5</margin> All this is because of the transgression of Jacob and because of the sin of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? Is it not Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Are they not Jerusalem?
<margin>6</margin> Therefore, I will make Samaria a heap of ruins in the open country, a place for planting vineyards. I will pour down her stones into the valley and uncover her foundations.
<margin>7</margin> All her carved images shall be beaten to pieces, and all her wages <note>original: "اعقارها" — referring to the hire or earnings of a harlot, symbolizing the wealth gained through idolatry.</note> shall be burned with fire. All her idols I will lay desolate, for she gathered them from the pay of a harlot, and to the pay of a harlot they shall return.
<margin>8</margin> For this I will wail and howl; I will go stripped and naked. I will make a wailing like the jackals and a mourning like the daughters of the ostrich <note>original: "رعال النعام" — likely referring to the shrill, mournful cry of young ostriches.</note>.
<margin>9</margin> For her wounds are incurable; for it has come even to Judah; it has reached the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.
<margin>10</margin> Tell it not in Gath, weep not at all in Akka <note>original: "عكاء" — likely referring to the city of Akko; the text uses wordplay between city names and the sounds of mourning.</note>. # Nahum
## Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> An oracle <note>original: "وحيٌ" (wahyun) — literally a "burden" or a heavy prophetic weight concerning a nation.</note> concerning Nineveh <note>The great capital of the Assyrian Empire, enemies of Israel.</note>. The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and will by no means clear the guilty. <margin>4</margin> The Lord has His way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of His feet. He rebukes the sea and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan and Carmel wither, and the flower of Lebanon fades. <margin>5</margin> The mountains quake before Him, the hills melt, and the earth heaves at His presence, yes, the world and all who dwell in it. <margin>6</margin> Who can stand before His indignation? And who can endure the fierceness of His anger?

## Chapter Two

<margin>1</margin> The shatterer <note>original: "المقمعة" (al-miqma'ah) — a term for a mace or a crushing weapon, personified here as an invading army.</note> has come up before your face. Guard the fortress! Watch the road! Strengthen your loins! Fortify your power greatly! <margin>2</margin> For the Lord restores the majesty of Jacob as the majesty of Israel, <margin>3</margin> for the plunderers have plundered them and ruined their vine branches. The shield of his mighty men is made red; the valiant men are in scarlet. The chariots flash with the fire of steel in the day of his preparation, and the cypress spears are brandished.
<margin>4</margin> The chariots rage in the streets, they rush to and fro in the broad ways; their appearance is like torches, they run like lightning.
<margin>5</margin> He summons his nobles; they stumble in their walk; they hasten to her wall, and the <margin>6-7</margin> protective pavise <note>A large shield or structure used by besiegers to protect themselves from arrows.</note> is prepared. The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace melts away. It is decreed <note>original: "وهصب" (wa-hussab) — a difficult Hebrew term often left as a proper name 'Huzzab' or interpreted as 'it is decreed'.</note>: she is stripped bare, she is carried away, and her handmaids moan like the voice of doves, beating upon their breasts. <margin>8</margin> And Nineveh is like a pool of water from of old; but now they flee. "Stand! Stand!" they cry, but no one looks back. <margin>9</margin> Plunder the silver! Plunder the gold! For there is no end to the treasure—an abundance of every desirable object. <margin>10</margin> She is empty, desolate, and waste!

### Chapter Three

<margin>1-2</margin> **Woe to the city of blood!** It is all full of lies and robbery; the preying never ceases. <margin>8</margin> Are you better than **No-Amon** <note>original: "نوآمون" (No-Amon), the ancient Egyptian city of Thebes.</note> that sat among the rivers, with waters around her, whose <margin>9</margin> rampart was the sea, and whose wall was the sea? **Cush** <note>original: "كوش" (Cush), referring to the region of modern-day Ethiopia and Sudan.</note> and **Egypt** <note>original: "مصر" (Misr).</note> were her strength, and it was boundless; **Put** <margin>10</margin> and the **Libyans** <note>original: "لوبيم" (Lubim).</note> were your helpers. You also will be drunk; you will be hidden; you also will seek a stronghold because of the enemy.

## Haggai

### Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> In the second year of King Darius, in the sixth month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of <margin>2</margin> Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, saying: * “Thus speaks the Lord of hosts, saying: This people says, ‘The time has not yet come, the time for the house of the Lord to be built.’”
<margin>3-4</margin> Then the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet, saying: * “Is it time for you yourselves <margin>5</margin> to dwell in your paneled houses <note>original: "المغشاة"; referring to luxury wood-paneling or ceilings, contrasting the finished state of personal homes with the ruins of the Temple.</note> while this house lies in ruins? * Now therefore, thus says the Lord of <margin>6</margin> hosts: Consider your ways! * You have sown much, and harvested little; you eat, but do not have enough; you drink, but you are not filled; you clothe yourselves, but no one is warm; and he who earns wages, earns wages to put into a bag with holes.”

<margin>7-8</margin> Thus says the Lord of hosts: “Consider your ways! * Go up to the mountain and bring wood and build the house, that I may take pleasure in it and be glorified,” says the Lord. <margin>9</margin> “You looked for much, and indeed it came to little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why?” says the Lord of hosts. “Because of my house which is in ruins, while every one of you runs to his own house. <margin>10</margin> Therefore the heavens above you withhold the dew, and the earth withholds its fruit. <margin>11</margin> And I called for a drought <note>original: "بالحر"; literally 'heat,' used here to denote a divine decree of drought affecting the harvest.</note> on the land and the mountains, on the grain and the new wine <note>original: "المسطار"; an archaic term for newly pressed grape juice.</note>, on the oil, on whatever the ground brings forth, on men and livestock, and on all the labor of the hands.”

<summary>This page concludes the Book of Zephaniah's promise of restoration and begins the Book of Haggai, where the prophet rebukes the returned exiles for prioritizing their own luxurious homes over the reconstruction of God's Temple.</summary>

## Chapter Eleven

<margin>1-3</margin> Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may devour your cedars. * Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty are ruined. ## Chapter Thirteen

<margin>1</margin> In that day, there shall be a fountain <note>original: "ينبوع" (yanbu'); a source of flowing water, symbolizing life and spiritual washing.</note> opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for impurity. <margin>2</margin> "And it shall be in that day," says the Lord of hosts, "that I will cut off the names of the idols from the land, and they shall no longer be remembered. I will also remove the prophets and the unclean spirit <note>original: "الروح النجس" (al-ruh al-najis); a reference to the spirit of falsehood or demonic influence that prompted false prophecy.</note> from the land. <margin>3</margin> And it shall be that if anyone still prophesies, his father and his mother who bore him will say to him, 'You shall not live, because you have spoken lies in the name of the Lord.' And his father and mother who bore him shall pierce him through when he prophesies. <margin>4</margin> And it shall be in that day that the prophets will each be ashamed of his vision when he prophesies; <margin>5</margin> they will not wear a hairy mantle <note>original: "ثوب شعر" (thawb sha'r); the traditional garment of a prophet, such as that worn by Elijah or John the Baptist, used here to denote someone trying to look the part of a holy man.</note> in order to deceive. Rather, he will say, 'I am no prophet. I am a tiller of the ground, for a man has kept me in bondage <note>original: "اقتناني" (iqtanani); can mean bought, possessed, or assigned to labor.</note> from my youth.' <margin>6</margin> And if someone says to him, 'What are these wounds in your hands?' <note>original: "الجروح في يديك" (al-juruh fi yadayk); interpreted by some as signs of mourning or pagan rituals, and by others as a Messianic foreshadowing.</note> then he will answer, 'Those with which I was wounded in the house of my friends.'</margin>

<margin>7</margin> "Awake, O sword, against My shepherd, and against the man who is My companion," <note>original: "رجل رفقتي" (rajul rifqati); implies a close associate or one who stands next to God.</note> says the Lord of hosts. "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered; and I will turn My hand against the little ones. <margin>8</margin> And it shall come to pass in all the land," says the Lord, "that two-thirds in it shall be cut off and die, but one-third shall be left in it. <margin>9</margin> And I will bring the one-third through the fire, and refine them as silver is refined, and test them as gold is tested. They will call on My name, and I will answer them. I will say, 'This is My people,' and they will say, 'The Lord is my God.'"

## Chapter Fourteen

<margin>1-2</margin> Behold, a day of the Lord is coming, when your spoil will be divided in your midst. For I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem to battle; the city shall be taken, the houses plundered, and the women ravished. Half of the city shall go into captivity <term>captivity: "السبي" (al-saby); the forced removal of a population, a recurring theme in Israel's history.</term>, but the remnant of the people shall not be cut off from the city. <margin>3-4</margin> Then the Lord will go forth and fight against those nations, as when He fights in the day of battle. And in that day His feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives, which faces Jerusalem on the east. And the Mount of Olives shall be split in two, from east to west, making a very large valley.

<note>The vocabulary section below highlights key terms found in the text.</note>
<term>Zechariah</term>: The prophet whose name means "Yahweh has remembered."
<term>Jerusalem</term>: The central holy city and focus of these prophecies.
<term>Lord of Hosts</term>: A divine title emphasizing God's command over heavenly and earthly armies.
<term>Prophets</term>: Those who speak on behalf of God; here, the text warns against false ones.
<term>Mount of Olives</term>: A ridge east of Jerusalem, significant in both Old and New Testament theology.
<term>Captivity</term>: Exile or imprisonment of a nation.
<term>Day of Battle</term>: A reference to decisive divine intervention in history.

## Chapter Two

<margin>1-2</margin> And now, O priests, this commandment is for you. * If you will not listen, and if you will not take it to heart to give glory to My name, says the Lord of Hosts, I will send a curse upon you, and I will curse <margin>3</margin> your blessings. Yes, I have cursed them already, because you do not take it to heart. * Behold, I will rebuke your offspring <note>original: "الزرع" (al-zar'); literally "the seed," referring here to the descendants or the future harvest.</note> and spread offal <note>original: "الفرث" (al-farth); the contents of the stomach and intestines of sacrificed animals, considered unclean and humiliating when applied to the face.</note> on your faces—the offal of your feasts; and you will be taken away with it. <margin>4</margin> Then you shall know that I have sent this commandment to you, that My covenant with Levi <note>The tribe designated for the priesthood.</note> might continue, says the Lord of Hosts. <margin>5</margin> My covenant with him was one of life and peace, and I gave them to him that he might fear Me. So he feared Me and stood in awe of My name. <margin>6</margin> The law of truth was in his mouth, and injustice was not found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and equity, and turned many away from iniquity. <margin>7</margin> For the lips of a priest should preserve knowledge, and people should seek the law <note>original: "الشريعة" (al-shari'a); divine instruction or the Torah.</note> from his mouth; for he is the messenger of the Lord of Hosts. <margin>8</margin> But you have departed from the way; you have caused many to stumble at the law. You have corrupted the covenant of Levi, says the Lord of Hosts. <margin>9</margin> Therefore I also have made you contemptible and base before all the people, because you have not kept My ways but have shown partiality in the law.

## Chapter Twelve

<margin>1</margin> At that time, Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry <margin>2</margin> and began to pluck heads of grain and eat. When the Pharisees <note>A Jewish sect known for strict adherence to the traditional and written Law.</note> saw this, they said to him, "Look, your disciples <margin>3</margin> are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath." * But he said to them, "Have you not read what David did when <margin>4</margin> he and those with him were hungry? * How he entered the house of God and ate the showbread <term>showbread: original: خبز التقدمة (khubz al-taqdima); twelve loaves of holy bread set out before God in the Temple, reserved strictly for priests.</term> which was not <margin>5</margin> lawful for him to eat, nor for those with him, but only for the priests? * Or have you not read in the Torah <note>original: التوراة (al-Tawrah); the first five books of the Hebrew Bible containing the Law of Moses.</note> that on the Sabbath the priests <margin>6</margin> in the temple profane the Sabbath and yet are innocent? * But I say to you that <margin>7</margin> something greater than the temple is here. * If you had known what this means: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice,' you would not have <margin>8</margin> condemned the innocent. * For the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath as well."

<margin>9</margin> Then he departed from there and went into their synagogue. * And behold, there was a man with a withered hand. So they asked him, <margin>10</margin> saying, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?"—so that they might bring a charge against him. * He said to them, "What <margin>11</margin> man among you, if he has one sheep and it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, <margin>12</margin> will he not take hold of it and lift it out? * How much more valuable is a man than a sheep! Therefore, it is lawful to do <margin>13</margin> good on the Sabbath." * Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He stretched it out, and it was restored to health like the other.

"For this reason, I speak to them in parables. <margin>24</margin> He presented another parable to them, saying: "The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed <margin>25</margin> in his field. * But while men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds <note>original: زواناً (zuwānan); specifically referring to *Lolium temulentum* or "darnel," a poisonous weed that looks identical to wheat in its early stages.</note> in the midst of the wheat and went away.

So the servants said to him, 'Do you want us to go <margin>29</margin> and gather them?' * But he said, 'No, lest while you gather the weeds, you uproot the wheat with them. <margin>30</margin> * Let them both grow together until the harvest. And at the time of harvest, I will say to the harvesters: "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my storehouse."'"

But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the cities.

## Chapter Sixteen

<margin>1</margin> And after the Sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought <margin>2</margin> spices <note>original: "حنوطاً" (hanut), aromatic oils and ointments used to prepare a body for burial</note> that they might come and anoint him. And very early in the morning, on the first day of the week, they came to the tomb as the sun <margin>3</margin> had risen. And they were saying among themselves, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the door of the tomb?" <margin>4-5</margin> But when they looked up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was very large. And entering the <margin>6</margin> tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, clothed in a white robe, and they were amazed. And he said to them, "Do not be amazed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. <margin>7</margin> See the place where they laid him. But go, tell his disciples and Peter that <margin>8</margin> he is going before you into Galilee; there you will see him, as he said to you." So they went out <insert>quickly</insert> and fled from the tomb, for trembling and bewilderment had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.

<margin>9</margin> Now when he had risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had <margin>10</margin> cast out seven demons. She went and told those who had been with him, as <margin>11</margin> they mourned and wept. And when those people heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe. <margin>12</margin> After that, he appeared in another form to two of them as they walked, heading into the <margin>13</margin> countryside <note>original: "البرية" (al-barriyya), referring to the open fields or rural areas outside the city</note>. And these two went and told the rest, but they did not believe them either. <margin>14</margin> Finally, he appeared to the eleven as they sat at the table <note>original: "متكئون" (muttaki'un), describing the ancient custom of reclining on couches during a meal</note>; and he rebuked their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they <margin>15</margin> did not believe those who had seen him after he had risen. And he said to them, "Go into all the world and preach <margin>16</margin> the Gospel <note>original: "الانجيل" (al-injil), derived from the Greek 'euangelion' meaning 'good news'</note> to every creature. He who believes and is baptized will be saved; but he who does not believe will be condemned. <margin>17</margin> And these signs will follow those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak with new <margin>18</margin> tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will by no means hurt them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will recover."

<margin>19</margin> So then, after the Lord had spoken to them, he was received up into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God. <margin>20</margin> And they went out and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs. (Amen)

<term>Gospel of Luke</term>: The third of the four canonical Gospels, traditionally attributed to Luke the physician.
<term>Zechariah</term>: A priest of the order of Abijah and the father of John the Baptist.
<term>Elizabeth</term>: The wife of Zechariah and mother of John the Baptist; she was a relative of Mary, the mother of Jesus.
<term>John</term>: Refers to John the Baptist, the forerunner of Jesus.
<term>Gabriel</term>: An archangel who serves as a messenger from God.
<term>Herod</term>: Herod the Great, the Roman-appointed king of Judea.
<term>Theophilus</term>: The individual to whom the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are addressed.
<term>Priesthood</term>: The organized body of priests who performed sacred rituals in the Temple.
<term>Angel of the Lord</term>: A divine messenger from God.
<term>Holy Spirit</term>: The third person of the Trinity in Christian theology, described here as empowering John from birth.

## Chapter Six

1 And on the Sabbath (the second after the first) <note>original: "الثاني بعد الأول" – a translation of the Greek term *deuteroproto*, referring to a specific point in the liturgical or harvest calendar</note> he passed through the grainfields. His disciples were plucking the heads of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands. * Some of the Pharisees said to them, "Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?" * Jesus answered and said to them, "Have you not even read this, which David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: * how he entered the house of God and took the bread of the Presence <note>original: "خبز التقدمة" – sacred bread set out in the sanctuary</note> and ate, and gave some to those with him also; which is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone?" * And he said to them, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath also."

6 On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and began to teach. A man was there whose right hand was withered. * The scribes and the Pharisees were watching him closely to see if he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a way to complain against him. * But he knew their thoughts and said to the man whose hand was withered, "Rise and stand in the center." So he rose and stood. * Then Jesus said to them, "I ask you one thing: Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil? To save a soul or to destroy it?" * Then he looked around at them all and said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." He did so, and his hand was restored <insert>healthy</insert> like the other. * But they were filled with fury <note>original: "حمقاً" – literally foolishness or senseless rage</note> and began to discuss among themselves what they might do to Jesus.

12 In those days, he went out to the mountain to pray, and spent the whole night in prayer to God. * When it was day, he called his disciples and chose twelve from among them, whom he also named Apostles: * Simon, whom he also named Peter, and Andrew his brother; James and John; Philip and Bartholomew; * Matthew and Thomas; James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who is called the Zealot <term>Zealot: a member of a Jewish political movement seeking independence from Roman rule</term>; * Judas <insert>brother of</insert> James, and Judas Iscariot, who also became a traitor.

17 He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a gathering of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea, Jerusalem, and the coast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases; * and those tormented by unclean spirits were being healed. * And the whole crowd sought to touch him, because power was going out from him and healing them all.

<margin>21</margin> have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.' So that servant came and reported these things to his master."

## Chapter Sixteen

1 And he also said to his disciples, "There was a certain rich man who had a steward <term>steward: "وكيل" (wakil) - an administrator or manager of a household or estate</term>, and an accusation was brought to him that this man was wasting

7 'A hundred baths <note>original: "بث" (bath) - an ancient liquid measure, approximately 8 to 9 gallons</note> of oil.' He said to him, 'Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty.' Then

8 eighty.' And the master praised the dishonest steward <term>dishonest steward: "وكيل الظلم" (wakil al-zulm) - literally 'the steward of injustice'</term> because he had acted shrewdly. For the sons of this age

# Gospel of John

### Chapter One

1-2 In the beginning was the Word <note>original: "al-Kalima," the Arabic translation of the Greek "Logos"</note>, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. * This was in the
3-4 beginning with God. * All things were made through him, and without him was not anything made that was made. * In him
5 was life, and the life was the light of men. * And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not
overcome it <note>The Arabic "tudrikuhu" can mean to grasp, to comprehend, or to overtake</note>.

<summary>The text concludes the Gospel of Luke with Jesus eating with his disciples to prove his physical resurrection and his subsequent ascension, followed by the iconic opening of the Gospel of John describing the eternal nature of "the Word."</summary>

<summary>Paul concludes his sermon by contrasting the corruptible body of King David with the resurrected Jesus, leading to a massive turnout the following Sabbath. Faced with Jewish opposition, Paul and Barnabas formally declare their mission to the Gentiles before being expelled from the city.</summary>

### Chapter Twenty

<margin>1</margin> After the uproar had ceased, Paul called the disciples to himself, embraced them, and departed to go to <term>Macedonia</term> <note>A Roman province in modern-day northern Greece.</note>. 

<margin>2</margin> Now when he had gone over those regions and encouraged them with many words, he came to <term>Hellas</term> <note>original: "هلاس"; the Greek name for Greece.</note>. 

<margin>3</margin> And he stayed there three months. When a plot was devised against him by the Jews as he was about to sail to Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. 

<margin>4</margin> And Sopater of Beroea accompanied him to Asia—also Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians, and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia. 

<margin>5-6</margin> These men went ahead and waited for us at <term>Troas</term> <note>A major port city in northwest Asia Minor.</note>. But we sailed away from Philippi after the <term>Days of Unleavened Bread</term> <note>A Jewish festival immediately following Passover.</note>, and in five days joined them at Troas, where we stayed seven days.

<margin>7</margin> Now on the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul, ready to depart the next day, spoke to them and continued his message until midnight. 

<margin>8</margin> There were many lamps in the upper room where they were gathered together. 

<margin>9</margin> And in a window sat a certain young man named <term>Eutychus</term>, who was sinking into a deep sleep. As Paul continued speaking for a long time, he was overcome by sleep and fell down from the third story, and was taken up dead. 

<margin>10</margin> But Paul went down, fell on him, and embracing him said, “Do not be troubled, for his life is in him.” 

<margin>11</margin> Now when he had come up, had broken bread and eaten, and talked a long while, even till daybreak, he departed. 

<margin>12</margin> And they brought the young man in alive, and they were not a little comforted.

### Chapter Three

<margin>1-2</margin> Then what is the advantage of the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way.
<margin>3</margin> First, because they were entrusted with the words <note>original: "أقوال" (aqwal), referring to the divine oracles or revelations</note> of God. For what if some were not faithful? 
<margin>4</margin> Will their lack of faithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God? God forbid! Rather, let God be true and every human a liar, as it is written: "That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged."
<margin>5</margin> But if our unrighteousness demonstrates the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who brings 
<margin>6</margin> wrath? I speak in human terms <note>original: "اتكلم بحسب الانسان" (atkallam bi-hasab al-insan), a rhetorical device Paul uses to show he is using human logic to illustrate a point</note>. God forbid! For then how will God judge the world? 
<margin>7</margin> For if the truth of God has increased through my lie to His glory, why am I also still judged 
<margin>8</margin> as a sinner? And why not say (as we are slandered and as some claim we say), "Let us do evil that good may come"? Their condemnation is just.
<margin>9</margin> What then? Are we better? Not at all. For we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks 
<margin>10</margin> are all under sin. As it is written: "There is none righteous, no, not one; 
<margin>12</margin> there is none who understands; there is none who seeks God. They have all turned aside and together become corrupt; there is none who 
<margin>13</margin> does good, no, not one. Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they have practiced deceit; 
<margin>14-15</margin> the poison of asps <note>original: "الاصلال" (al-aslal), referring to venomous snakes</note> is under their lips; and their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to 
<margin>16-17</margin> shed blood; in their ways are ruin and robbery; and the way of peace they have not known. 
<margin>18-19</margin> There is no fear of God before their eyes." Now we know that whatever the Law <term>Law: "الناموس" (al-namus), referring here to the Mosaic Law or the Old Testament scriptures</term> says, it speaks to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and all the world may become subject to 
<margin>20</margin> punishment from God. For by the works of the Law no flesh <note>original: "كل ذي جسد" (kull dhi jasad), literally 'every possessor of a body,' meaning every human being</note> will be justified in His sight, for through the Law comes the knowledge of sin.
<margin>21</margin> But now the righteousness of God apart from the Law has been revealed, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets; 
<margin>22</margin> the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ to all and upon all who believe. For there is no difference; 
<margin>23-24</margin> for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, being justified freely by His grace through the redemption <term>redemption: "الفداء" (al-fida'), the act of buying back or liberating</term> 
<margin>25</margin> that is in Jesus Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation <term>propitiation: "كفّارة" (kaffarah), an atoning sacrifice that satisfies divine justice</term> through faith in His blood, to demonstrate His righteousness...

<summary>In this passage, Paul argues that while the Jewish people have a historical advantage in receiving God's word, they are still subject to sin like the rest of humanity. He concludes that no one can be justified by following the Law alone, but only through faith in the redemption provided by Jesus Christ.</summary>

### Chapter Four

<margin>1-2</margin> Thus let a man account of us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries <term>mysteries: "سرائر" (sara'ir); refers to the deep truths of God's plan once hidden but now revealed</term> of God. * Moreover, it is required of 
<margin>3</margin> stewards that a man be found faithful. * But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged 
<margin>4</margin> by you or by a human day <term>human day: "يوم بشر" (yawm bashar); a Hebrew/Semitic idiom referring to a human court or judgment day</term>. Indeed, I do not even judge myself. * For I am not aware 
of anything against myself, yet I am not thereby justified. But He who judges me is 
<margin>5</margin> the Lord. * Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will enlighten 
the hidden things of darkness and reveal the intentions of the hearts. And then each one will have praise from God.

6 Now these things, brothers, I have figuratively applied to myself and to Apollos for your sakes, so that you may learn through us not to think beyond what is written, so that none of you may be puffed up <note>meaning arrogant or prideful</note> on behalf of one against the other. 7 For who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive? Now if you did indeed receive it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? 8 You are already full! You have already become rich! You have reigned as kings without us—and I wish indeed that you did reign, so that we might also reign with you! 9 For I think that God has displayed us, the apostles, as the last of all, as those condemned to death; for we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to men. 10 We are fools for the sake of Christ, but you are wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are strong! You are honored, but we are without honor! 11 To this very hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly clothed and beaten, and we have no permanent home. 12 And we labor, working with our own hands. When we are reviled, we bless; when we are persecuted, we endure; 13 when we are slandered, we encourage. We have become like the filth of the world and the offscouring of all things <note>referring to the most discarded or worthless refuse</note> until now. 14 I do not write these things to shame you, but as my beloved children I warn you. 15 For even if you had ten thousand <term>instructors</term> <note>original: مرشدين; referring to tutors or guardians who oversaw children</note> in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For I became your father in Christ Jesus through the <term>Gospel</term> <note>original: الانجيل; the "Good News" of the Christian message</note>. 16 Therefore I urge you, be imitators of me. 17 For this reason I sent to you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach everywhere in every church. 18 Now some have become puffed up, as if I were not coming to you. 19 But I will come to you shortly, if the Lord wills, and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. 20 For the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. 21 What do you desire? Shall I come to you with a rod <note>symbolizing discipline or punishment</note>, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

## Chapter Five

1 It is widely reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles—that a man has his father’s wife! 2 And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from among you. 3 For I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged the one who has committed this act, as if I were present. 4 In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

1 ⁠Does any of you, having a grievance against another, dare to go to law before the <term>unrighteous</term> <note>original: الظالمين; here referring to secular or pagan judges who do not share the community's spiritual values</note> and not before the <term>saints</term> <note>original: القديسين; a term Paul frequently uses for all members of the church, meaning "set apart ones," rather than specifically canonized figures.</note>? 2 ⁠Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? ## Chapter Seven

<margin>1</margin>Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: "It is good for a man not to touch <margin>2</margin>a woman" <note>This likely quotes a slogan or a specific question sent to Paul by the Corinthians who were debating the merits of total celibacy.</note>. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise, the husband does not have authority <margin>5</margin>over his own body, but the wife does. Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may devote yourselves (to fasting and) prayer; then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. <margin>6</margin>But I say this as a concession <note>original: اذن; meaning Paul is giving permission or advice rather than issuing a divine decree.</note>, not as a <margin>7</margin>command. I wish that all people were as I myself am. But each has his own special gift from God, one of one kind and another of another.

in all things. They do it to receive a crown that perishes <note>original: اكليلاً يفنى (iklilan yafna); likely referring to the laurel wreaths given at the Isthmian Games in Corinth, which would eventually wither.</note>, but we, a crown that does not perish.

<summary>Paul explains that while he has a right to financial support for his ministry, he chooses to waive it to avoid hindering the Gospel. He uses athletic metaphors—running and boxing—to emphasize the necessity of self-discipline in the Christian life.</summary>

<summary>Paul contrasts the fading glory of the Mosaic Law with the enduring, transformative glory of the New Covenant in the Spirit. He argues that while many remain "veiled" to the truth, his ministry is conducted with transparency and sincerity before God.</summary>

Following the previous page's discussion on the "New Covenant" and the "ministry of the Spirit," Paul now addresses how divine light overcomes the darkness of the world and how the temporary suffering of the physical body compares to the eternal glory of the afterlife.</meta>

6 [For the sake of] Jesus. For it is God, who said, "Let light shine out of darkness," who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
<margin>7-8</margin> But we have this treasure in earthen vessels <note>original: اوانٍ خزفية (awānin khazafiyya); a metaphor comparing the human body to fragile clay pots that nonetheless contain the priceless "treasure" of the Gospel.</note> so that the excellence of the power may be from God and not from us. We are hard-pressed
<margin>9</margin> 9 in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted,
<margin>10</margin> 10 but not abandoned; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body
<margin>11</margin> 11 the dying of the Lord Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body. For we
the living are always being given over to death for Jesus' sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in
<margin>12</margin> 12 our mortal flesh. So then death is at work in us, but life in you. Since we have
the same spirit of faith according to what is written: "I believed, and therefore I spoke." We also believe
<margin>14</margin> 14 and therefore speak, knowing that He who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us
<margin>15</margin> 15 with Jesus and present us with you. For all things are for your sake, so that grace,
<margin>16</margin> 16 as it extends to more and more people, may increase thanksgiving to the glory of God. Therefore we do not lose heart; even though
<margin>17</margin> 17 our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day. For our light, momentary affliction
<margin>18</margin> 18 is producing for us an eternal weight of glory far beyond all comparison, as we look not at the things which are
seen but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

## Chapter Five

<margin>1</margin> 1 For we know that if our earthly house, this tent <note>original: خيمتنا (khaymatinā); Paul frequently uses tent-making imagery—his own trade—to describe the temporary nature of the human body.</note>, is destroyed, we have a building from
<margin>2</margin> 2 God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this tent we groan, longing to
<margin>3</margin> 3 be clothed with our dwelling from heaven; and if we have put it on, we will not be found naked.
<margin>4</margin> 4 For we who are in this tent groan, being burdened, not because we want to be unclothed, but rather
<margin>5</margin> 5 to be clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now He who has prepared us for this very thing is
<margin>6</margin> 6 God, who also has given us the <term>guarantee of the Spirit</term> <note>original: عربون الروح (ʿurbūn al-rūḥ); the word "ʿurbūn" refers to a down payment or earnest money that guarantees the full transaction will be completed later.</note>. Therefore we are always confident, knowing
<margin>7</margin> 7 that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord. For by faith
<margin>8</margin> 8 we walk, not by sight. We are confident, and well-pleased rather to be absent from the body and to be at home with [the Lord].

<summary>Paul discusses the contrast between the fragile "earthen vessels" of human life and the "eternal weight of glory" awaiting believers, using the metaphor of a tent to describe the temporary nature of the physical body.</summary>

<margin>6</margin> conflicts without, fears within. <note>Paul is describing the intense psychological and physical pressure he faced before reuniting with his companion.</note> But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us 
<margin>7</margin> by the coming of Titus. And not only by his coming, but also by the comfort with which he was comforted because of you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.

<margin>12</margin> yourselves to be clear in this matter. Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who was wronged, but that our care for you might be revealed to you before God.

<margin>15</margin> our boasting to Titus proved true. And his heart overflows with even more affection toward you as he remembers the 
<margin>16</margin> obedience of you all, and how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice (therefore) that I have confidence in you in everything.

### Chapter Nine

<margin>1-2</margin> For concerning the <term>service to the saints</term> <note>original: "الخدمة للقديسيين" (al-khidmah lil-qiddisin). This refers to the relief fund being collected for the impoverished church in Jerusalem.</note>, it is superfluous for me to write to you; for I know your willingness, of which I boast about you to the Macedonians, that <term>Achaia</term> <note>original: "اخائية" (Akha'iyyah). A Roman province in southern Greece where Corinth was the capital.</note> has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up the majority.

<margin>3</margin> Yet I have sent the brothers, lest our boasting about you should be in vain in this respect, that, as I said, you may be ready;

<margin>4</margin> lest if some Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to mention you!—should be ashamed in this confident boasting.

<margin>5</margin> Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brothers to go to you ahead of time, and prepare your generous <term>blessing</term> <note>original: "بركتكم" (barakatakum). Paul uses the word 'blessing' to describe their financial gift, emphasizing it as an act of grace rather than a tax.</note> which was previously promised, that it may be ready as a matter of generosity and not as a matter of greed.

<margin>6</margin> But this I say: He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows with blessings will also reap with blessings.

<margin>7</margin> So let each one give as he purposes in his heart, not grudgingly or of necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver.

<margin>8</margin> And God is able to make all grace abound toward you, that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may have an abundance for every good work.

<margin>9</margin> As it is written: “He has dispersed abroad; He has given to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.”

<margin>10</margin> Now may He who supplies seed to the sower, and bread for food, supply and multiply the seed you have sown and increase the fruits of your righteousness;

<margin>11</margin> while you are enriched in everything for all liberality, which causes thanksgiving through us to God.

<margin>12</margin> For the administration of this service not only supplies the needs of the saints, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to God,

<margin>13</margin> while, through the proof of this ministry, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Gospel of Christ, and for your liberal sharing with them and all men,

<margin>14</margin> and by their prayer for you, who long for you because of the exceeding grace of God in you.

<margin>15</margin> Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!

# The Second Epistle to the Corinthians * 10 * 11 *

I beg you that when I am present I may not be bold with that confidence by which I intend to be courageous against some who account us as if we
<margin>3</margin> <term>walk according to the flesh</term> <note>original: "نسلك حسب الجسد" (nasluk hasab al-jasad). To "walk according to the flesh" means to live or act by worldly, selfish, or human standards rather than by the Spirit of God.</note>. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to
<margin>4</margin> the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the
<margin>5</margin> pulling down of strongholds; pulling down arguments and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every
<margin>6</margin> thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ; and being ready to punish all disobedience when your 
->obedience<-
is complete.
<margin>7</margin> Do you look at things according to their outward appearance? If anyone is confident in himself that he is Christ’s, let him consider 
<margin>8</margin> this again from himself, that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we (Christ’s). For even if I
should boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave us for your building up and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed; 
<margin>10</margin> lest I appear as if I were terrifying you by my letters. For "the letters," he says, "are weighty and powerful, but his bodily 
<margin>11</margin> presence is weak and his speech contemptible." Let such a person consider this: that as we are in 
<margin>12</margin> word by letters when we are absent, such we will also be in deed when we are present. For we do not dare 
to count ourselves among or compare ourselves with those who commend themselves. But 
they, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, do not understand.
<margin>13</margin> But we will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the <term>rule</term> <note>original: "القانون" (al-qanun). This refers to a limit or a boundary of a specific geographical area or jurisdiction assigned to Paul by God.</note> which
<margin>14</margin> God has apportioned to us, a measure reaching even to you. For we are not extending ourselves as if we did not reach 
<margin>15</margin> you; for we have come even to you in the gospel of Christ; not boasting beyond 
measure in the labors of others, but having hope that as your faith increases, we shall be greatly enlarged among you 
<margin>16</margin> according to our rule, even more; to preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in things already prepared in 
<margin>17</margin> the rule of others. But "he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord." For it is not the one who commends 
<margin>18</margin> himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

# The Second Epistle to the Corinthians * 11 *

For as the serpent deceived Eve by its craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is
<margin>4</margin> in Christ. For if the one who comes preaches another Jesus whom we have not preached, or if you receive
<margin>5</margin> another spirit which you have not received, or another gospel which you have not accepted, you may well put up with it! For I 
<margin>6</margin> consider that I am not at all inferior to the <term>eminent apostles</term> <note>original: "فائقي الرسل" (fa'iqi al-rusul). This refers to the "super-apostles" or false teachers who claimed higher authority than Paul.</note>. Even if I am <term>unskilled in speech</term> <note>original: "عاميا في الكلام" (amiyan fi al-kalam). Paul acknowledges he lacks the formal Greek rhetorical training favored by his rivals, though his knowledge is deep.</note>,
yet I am not so in knowledge; but we have been clearly revealed to you in all things among all people.
<margin>7</margin> Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the
<margin>8</margin> gospel of God to you free of charge? I robbed other churches, taking wages from them for your service. And when
<margin>9</margin> I was present with you and was in need, I was not a burden to anyone; for my need was supplied by
the brothers who came from <term>Macedonia</term> <note>A Roman province in northern Greece.</note>. In everything I kept myself from being a burden 
<margin>10</margin> to you, and so I will keep myself. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting shall not be silenced in 
<margin>11</margin> the regions of <term>Achaia</term> <note>A Roman province in southern Greece, where Corinth is located.</note>. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows! But what I do, I will continue to do,
that I may cut off the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity to be regarded just as we are in the things of which they boast.
<margin>13</margin> For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the likeness of
<margin>14</margin> apostles of Christ. And no wonder! For Satan himself transforms himself into the likeness of an angel of
<margin>15</margin> light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also transform themselves into the likeness of ministers of righteousness,
whose end will be according to their works.
<margin>16</margin> I say again, let no one think me a fool. If otherwise, at least receive me as a fool, that I also may boast
<margin>17</margin> a little. What I speak, I speak not according to the Lord, but as it were, in foolishness, in
<margin>18</margin> this confidence of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I will boast
<margin>19</margin> also. For you gladly put up with fools, since you yourselves are wise! For you put up with it if

<margin>21</margin> exalts himself, if someone strikes you on the face. To our shame I say that

<margin>22</margin> also. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the seed of Abraham?

## Chapter Thirteen

<margin>1-2</margin>This is the third time I am coming to you. "By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established." <note>Paul is quoting Deuteronomy 19:15, a legal principle from the Torah requiring multiple witnesses to confirm a matter, here applying it to his repeated warnings to the community.</note> I have previously said, and I say beforehand—as if I were present the second time, and being absent now—(I write) to those who have sinned before and to all the rest, that if I come again 
<margin>3</margin>I will not spare * since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, who is not weak

<margin>6</margin>Christ is in you?—unless indeed you are disqualified <note>original: "مرفوضين" (marfudin) — literally rejected, failing a test, or cast away; used here to describe those who do not pass the "test" of faith.</note>. * But I trust that you will know that we 
<margin>7</margin>are not disqualified. * Now I pray to God that you do no evil, not that we should appear approved <note>original: "مزكين" (muzakkin) — those who have been justified, commended, or shown to be authentic.</note>, but that you should do what is honorable, even though we may seem disqualified.

<margin>10</margin>weak and you are strong. <margin>13</margin>kiss. * All the saints greet you.

# The Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Galatians

## Chapter One

<margin>1</margin> Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father who 
<margin>2-3</margin> raised Him from the dead— * and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia: * Grace 
<margin>4</margin> to you and peace from God the Father and from our Lord Jesus Christ, * who gave Himself for 
<margin>5</margin> our sins to deliver us from the present evil world, according to the will of God our Father, * to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. 

<margin>6</margin> I marvel that you are turning away so quickly from Him who called you by the grace of Christ 
<margin>7</margin> to another gospel, * which is not another; except that there are some who trouble you and want to 
<margin>8</margin> pervert the gospel of Christ. * But even if we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel to you than what 
<margin>9</margin> we have preached to you, let him be <term>anathema</term> <note>original: "اناثيما" (anathima) — a Greek word meaning "devoted to destruction" or "accursed." Paul uses this severe term to express that those distorting the Gospel are under divine judgment.</note>. * As we have said before, so now I say again: If anyone 
<margin>10</margin> preaches any other gospel to you than what you have received, let him be anathema. * For do I now seek the favor of men, or of God? Or do I seek to please men? For if I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ. 

<margin>11</margin> But I make known to you, brothers, that the gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. 
<margin>12</margin> For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came through the revelation of Jesus Christ. * For you have heard of my former conduct in <term>Judaism</term> <note>original: "الديانة اليهودية" (al-diyanah al-yahudiyyah) — literally "the Jewish religion." Paul refers to his life before his conversion when he was a strict observer of Jewish Law.</note>, that I persecuted the church of God excessively 
<margin>14</margin> and tried to destroy it. * And I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my <term>contemporaries</term> <note>original: "اترابي" (atrabī) — those of the same age or generation.</note> in my own 
<margin>15</margin> nation, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. * But when it pleased God, who 
<margin>16</margin> set me apart from my mother's womb and called me through His grace, * to reveal His Son in me, that I might preach Him among the <term>Gentiles</term> <note>original: "الامم" (al-umam) — literally "the nations," referring to all non-Jewish peoples.</note>, 
<margin>17</margin> I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood <note>This is a biblical idiom meaning "human beings" or "human advice." Paul is emphasizing that his commission came directly from God, not from human discussion.</note>, * nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles 
<margin>18</margin> before me; but I went to Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. * Then after three [years]...

<summary>Paul opens his letter to the Galatians by asserting his divine commission as an apostle and condemning those who preach a different gospel. He begins his autobiography, explaining that his message came via direct revelation rather than human instruction, and mentions his transition from a persecutor of the church to a preacher in Arabia and Damascus.</summary>

# The Epistle to the Galatians * 3 *

11 ... what is written in the book of the Law to be done by it <note>This concludes a quote from Deuteronomy 27:26, asserting that the Law requires perfect obedience.</note> * But it is evident that no one is justified 
12 by the Law before God, for "the righteous shall live by faith" <note>A reference to Habakkuk 2:4.</note> * However, the Law is not based on 
13 faith; rather, "the person who does these things shall live by them." * Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for our sake, because it is written: "Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree" <note>original: *khashaba* (wood/timber). Referring to the wooden cross as a sign of being cast out, based on Deuteronomy 21:23.</note> 
14 * so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the nations <note>original: *al-umam*, often translated as Gentiles or non-Jewish peoples.</note> in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. 
15 Brothers, I speak in human terms: no one annuls a covenant <note>original: *‘ahdan*. Paul uses the analogy of a legal contract or testament.</note> that has been ratified, even 
16 if it is only a human one, nor does anyone add to it. * Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. The Scripture does not say "and to offsprings," as if referring to many, but as if referring to one: "and to your offspring," which 
17 is Christ. * What I mean is this: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, 
18 does not revoke a covenant previously ratified by God toward Christ, so as to nullify the promise. * For if the inheritance comes from the Law, then it is no longer from a promise. But God granted it to Abraham through a promise. 
19 Why then the Law? It was added because of transgressions until the offspring should come to whom 
20 the promise was made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. * Now a mediator does not represent just one party, but 
21 God is one. * Is the Law then against the promises of God? God forbid! For if a law had been given 
22 that was able to give life, then righteousness <term>Righteousness: *al-birr*, refers to being in a right standing or "justified" before God.</term> would indeed have come through the Law. * But the Scripture has confined everyone 
23 under sin, so that the promise by faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. * But before faith came, we were kept under guard under the Law, confined until the faith 
24 that was to come should be revealed. * Thus, the Law was our tutor <note>original: *mu'addibuna*. This refers to a *paedagogus*, a household guardian who supervised children and led them to school.</note> to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. 
25 * But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor. * For you are all children of God 26 
27 through faith in Christ Jesus. * For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ <note>A metaphor for taking on a new identity or character, like changing clothes.</note>. 
28 * There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all 
29 one in Christ Jesus. * And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring and, according to the promise, heirs.

### Chapter Four

<margin>1</margin> Now I say that as long as the heir is a minor <note>original: *qasiran*. In a legal sense, a child who has not yet reached the age of maturity to claim an inheritance.</note>, he is no different from a slave, though he is the master of 
<margin>2</margin> all; * rather, he is under guardians and stewards until the time set by his father. 
<margin>3-4</margin> * Even so we, when we were minors, were enslaved under the basic principles of the world <note>original: *arkan al-alam*. This refers to the rudimentary or elemental spiritual systems, whether Jewish or pagan, that preceded Christ.</note>. * But when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the Law <term>The Law: *al-namus*, referring specifically to the Mosaic Law of the Old Testament</term>, 
<margin>5-6</margin> * to redeem those under the Law, that we might receive adoption. * And because you are sons, 
God sent the Spirit of His Son into your hearts, crying out, "Abba, Father!" <note>original: *ya aba al-ab*. Paul uses both the Aramaic "Abba" and the Greek "Pater" (translated here to Arabic/English) to show the intimacy of a child with a father.</note> 
<margin>7</margin> * So you are no longer a slave but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ. 
<margin>8</margin> But at that time, when you did not know God, you were enslaved to those who by nature are not gods. 
<margin>9</margin> * But now that you have come to know God—or rather are known by God—how is it that you are turning back again to the

<summary>Paul argues that believers have graduated from being "slaves" under the Law to being "heirs" and "sons" through Christ. He expresses deep concern that the Galatians are returning to ritualistic "basic principles" and uses the allegory of Abraham's two sons to distinguish between legalism and the promise.</summary>
